claims.statement: Koromodako is an octopus yōkai in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Koromodako adalah yōkai gurita dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: is a yōkai in the Japanese folklore. Although in the guise of a small octopus, it is said to expand and envelop boats and people.

claims.statement: It can expand from a small form and envelop boats.
claims.statement_id: Ia dapat membesar dari wujud kecil dan menyelubungi perahu.
claims.quote: Although in the guise of a small octopus, it is said to expand and envelop boats and people.

claims.statement: Its legends are associated with northern Kyoto.
claims.statement_id: Legendanya dikaitkan dengan Kyoto utara.
claims.quote: The lore is localized in northern Kyoto Prefecture, vaguely described as promontory areas (jutting into Wakasa Bay)

claims.statement: It is said to sink vessels and their passengers.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon menenggelamkan kapal beserta penumpangnya.
claims.quote: As the name indicates, koromo-dako is an octopus-like yōkai that appear small at first, but expands widely like a piece of clothing when a boat arrives, and sinks both vessel and humans in the sea.

claims.statement: After feeding, it returns to a tiny form.
claims.statement_id: Setelah makan, ia kembali ke wujud kecil.
claims.quote: After feeding, the koromodako shrinks down to its tiny size, impossible to trace.

claims.statement: Some accounts place it within a shell.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian kisah menempatkannya di dalam cangkang.
claims.quote: Some of them are found concealed inside a shell.

claims.statement: Kuni-no-Satsuchi is a deity in the creation account of the Nihon Shoki.
claims.statement_id: Kuni-no-Satsuchi adalah dewa dalam kisah penciptaan Nihon Shoki.
claims.quote: 主に『日本書紀』の天地開闢の段に登場する神で別名国狭立尊（くにのさたちのみこと）。神代七代のうちの一柱である。

claims.statement: The deity belongs to the Seven Generations of the Age of Gods.
claims.statement_id: Dewa itu termasuk Tujuh Generasi Zaman Dewa.
claims.quote: 主に『日本書紀』の天地開闢の段に登場する神で別名国狭立尊（くにのさたちのみこと）。神代七代のうちの一柱である。

claims.statement: Kuni-no-Satachi is another name of this deity.
claims.statement_id: Kuni-no-Satachi adalah nama lain dewa ini.
claims.quote: 主に『日本書紀』の天地開闢の段に登場する神で別名国狭立尊（くにのさたちのみこと）。神代七代のうちの一柱である。

claims.statement: The main account places this male deity after Kuninotokotachi and before Toyokumono.
claims.statement_id: Kisah utama menempatkan dewa laki-laki ini setelah Kuninotokotachi dan sebelum Toyokumono.
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』本文では、天地開闢の後国常立尊、国狭槌尊が登場し、次に豊斟渟尊が化生したとしており、これらの三柱の神は男神であると記している。

claims.statement: In the first, second and fourth alternate accounts, Kuni no Satsuchi appears after Kuninotokotachi; the other accounts have no name regarded as the same deity, and he does not appear again in the myths of the Nihon Shoki.
claims.statement_id: Dalam riwayat pertama, kedua, dan keempat (isshō), Kuni no Satsuchi muncul setelah Kuninotokotachi; riwayat lain tidak memuat nama yang tampak sama, dan sesudah itu ia tidak muncul lagi dalam mitos Nihon Shoki.
claims.quote: 第一、第二と第四の一書では、国常立尊の次に国狭槌尊が登場し、他の一書には同一神とみられる神名は登場しない。 ... 『日本書紀』にこれ以降、国狭槌尊が神話に登場することはない。

claims.statement: The name "Satsuchi" may be read as "sa" (sacred rice) and "tsuchi" (earth), that is, the soil in which sacred rice is planted.
claims.statement_id: Nama "Satsuchi" mungkin dapat dipahami sebagai "sa" (padi suci) dan "tsuchi" (tanah), yakni tanah tempat padi suci ditanam.
claims.quote: 神名「サツチ」の「サ」は神稲、「ツチ」は土、即ち神稲を植える土の意か。

claims.statement: The Kojiki has Ame no Satsuchi and Kuni no Satsuchi as children of Ōyamatsumi, but neither is counted among the Seven Generations of the Age of Gods.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki memuat Ame no Satsuchi dan Kuni no Satsuchi sebagai anak Ōyamatsumi, tetapi keduanya tidak dihitung dalam Tujuh Generasi Zaman Dewa.
claims.quote: 『古事記』には大山津見神の子に天之狭土神・国之狭土神がいるが、どちらも神代七代に数えられていない。

claims.statement: The deity is enshrined at, among others, Kumano Hayatama Taisha in Wakayama, Naemura Shrine in Shiga (main deity) and Kunisatsuchi Shrine in Shiga (main deity).
claims.statement_id: Dewa ini dipuja antara lain di Kumano Hayatama Taisha (Wakayama), Naemura Jinja (Shiga; dewa utama), dan Kunisatsuchi Jinja (Shiga; dewa utama).
claims.quote: 熊野速玉大社（和歌山県新宮市新宮）‐一万宮祭神 苗村神社（滋賀県蒲生郡竜王町）‐主祭神 国狭槌神社（滋賀県高島市）‐主祭神

claims.statement: According to the Kokugakuin University Kojiki database, in the Nihon Shoki traditions Kuni no Satsuchi appears as the second deity after Kuninotokotachi among the first three deities to arise; one interpretation takes the name to mean an elder deity who manages all paddy-rice cultivation.
claims.statement_id: Menurut basis data Kojiki Universitas Kokugakuin, dalam berbagai riwayat Nihon Shoki Kuni no Satsuchi tampil sebagai dewa kedua setelah Kuninotokotachi di antara tiga dewa yang pertama muncul; satu tafsir memahaminya sebagai dewa sesepuh yang mengatur seluruh budi daya padi sawah.
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』の諸伝には、天地開闢で初めて生じた三神の内、国常立尊に次ぐ第二神として、類似の名を持つ「国狭槌尊（くにのさつちのみこと）」が登場する。この神に関する説としては、サを神稲、ツを助詞、チを生活や社会に必要な品々に関する経済活動を掌握する長老を表わす語と取り、水稲耕作の一切を掌握管理する長老の神と解する説がある。

claims.statement: In Aston's translation of the Nihongi, Kuni no sa-tsuchi no Mikoto comes next, then Toyo-kumu-nu, three deities in all.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston atas Nihongi, Kuni no sa-tsuchi no Mikoto muncul berikutnya, lalu Toyo-kumu-nu; seluruhnya tiga dewa.
claims.quote: Next there was Kuni no sa-tsuchi no Mikoto, and next Toyo-kumu-nu no Mikoto, in all three deities.

claims.statement: In one of the alternate accounts of the Nihongi, this deity is also called Kuni no sa-tachi no Mikoto.
claims.statement_id: Dalam salah satu riwayat tambahan Nihongi, dewa ini juga disebut Kuni no sa-tachi no Mikoto.
claims.quote: Next there was Kuni no sa-tsuchi no Mikoto, also called Kuni no sa-tachi no Mikoto.

claims.statement: One alternate account in the Nihongi says the deities were produced together: first Kuni-no-toko-tachi, then Kuni no sa-tsuchi.
claims.statement_id: Satu riwayat tambahan Nihongi menyebut para dewa itu dihasilkan bersama-sama: pertama Kuni-no-toko-tachi, lalu Kuni no sa-tsuchi.
claims.quote: When Heaven and Earth began, there were Deities produced together, whose names were, first, Kuni-no-toko-tachi no Mikoto, and next Kuni no sa-tsuchi no Mikoto.

claims.statement: Kyōkotsu is a yōkai in an Edo-period illustrated collection by Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Kyōkotsu adalah yōkai dalam kumpulan ilustrasi zaman Edo karya Sekien.
claims.quote: 狂骨（きょうこつ）は、鳥山石燕による江戸時代の妖怪画集『今昔百鬼拾遺』にある妖怪。平成以降は、京極夏彦による小説『狂骨の夢』でも知られる。

claims.statement: Its illustration shows a white-haired skeleton in a white garment.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasinya memperlihatkan kerangka berambut putih dengan pakaian putih.
claims.quote: 白髪の生えた骸骨姿の者が、白い衣を纏った幽霊のように、井戸の中から釣瓶に吊られて浮かび上がった姿が描かれており、解説文には以下のように述べられている。

claims.statement: The figure rises from a well attached to a bucket.
claims.statement_id: Sosok itu muncul dari sumur sambil tergantung pada ember.
claims.quote: 白髪の生えた骸骨姿の者が、白い衣を纏った幽霊のように、井戸の中から釣瓶に吊られて浮かび上がった姿が描かれており、解説文には以下のように述べられている。

claims.statement: Sekien’s description mentions intense resentment without identifying its precise nature.
claims.statement_id: Keterangan Sekien menyebut dendam yang kuat tanpa menjelaskan sifat tepatnya.
claims.quote: この解説においては、狂骨は井戸から現れることと、凄まじい怨みを持っていることが語られているが、それ以上の説明はなく、具体的にどのような妖怪を描いたものかは判明していない。

claims.statement: A later account has it arise from bones discarded in a well.
claims.statement_id: Kisah belakangan menyebutnya muncul dari tulang yang dibuang ke sumur.
claims.quote: Kyōkotsu are formed from bones which were improperly disposed of by being discarded down a well.

claims.statement: That account has it curse those who disturb its well.
claims.statement_id: Kisah itu menyebutnya mengutuk orang yang mengganggu sumurnya.
claims.quote: A kyōkotsu lies at the bottom of its well until it is disturbed, then it rises up to curse anyone unfortunate enough to be using the well.

claims.statement: Makuragaeshi is a Japanese spirit or yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Makuragaeshi adalah roh atau yōkai Jepang.
claims.quote: The makuragaeshi (枕返し or 反枕, “pillow flip”) is a kind of Japanese spirit or yōkai.

claims.statement: It is said to turn over a sleeper’s pillow at night.
claims.statement_id: Ia konon membalik bantal orang yang tidur pada malam hari.
claims.quote: They would come at night to one's pillow side and flip over the pillow.

claims.statement: Other accounts have it reverse the position of a sleeper’s head and feet.
claims.statement_id: Kisah lain menyebutnya menukar posisi kepala dan kaki orang yang tidur.
claims.quote: They are also considered to change which direction one's head or feet are facing.

claims.statement: Its appearance varies, sometimes resembling a child or monk.
claims.statement_id: Penampilannya beragam, kadang menyerupai anak atau biksu.
claims.quote: They are often found in many actual stories from the Edo Period to the modern period, and they are often said to appear as a small child or a bōzu, but there are no clear-cut accounts of how they look.

claims.statement: An Edo-period illustration depicts a miniature Niō guardian.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi zaman Edo menggambarkannya sebagai penjaga Niō kecil.
claims.quote: In the Edo Period collection of yōkai pictures, the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, they are depicted as a miniature Niō.

claims.statement: An origin story makes it the ghost of someone who died in the room.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita asal menjadikannya hantu seseorang yang meninggal di kamar itu.
claims.quote: Most often they linked to the ghosts of people — particularly children — who died in the room they come to haunt.

claims.statement: Miage-nyūdō is a yōkai of Sado Island.
claims.statement_id: Miage-nyūdō adalah yōkai dari Pulau Sado.
claims.quote: Miage-nyūdō is a type of yōkai told about on Sado Island (Sado, Niigata Prefecture).

claims.statement: It is classified as a kind of mikoshi-nyūdō.
claims.statement_id: Ia digolongkan sebagai jenis mikoshi-nyūdō.
claims.quote: They are a type of mikoshi-nyūdō.

claims.statement: The figure grows taller when a traveler looks up at it.
claims.statement_id: Sosok itu bertambah tinggi ketika pelancong mendongak melihatnya.
claims.quote: When climbing a small slope at night, something taking on the appearance of a little bōzu would appear in front, and by looking up, it would become taller, and the person looking at it would fall down backwards.

claims.statement: A formula declaring that its trick has been seen through is said to dispel it.
claims.statement_id: Ucapan bahwa tipuannya telah diketahui konon mengusirnya.
claims.quote: It is said that by chanting "miage-nyūdō, I've seen past you (見上入道、見越した )" and lying down forwards, it would disappear.

claims.statement: A Hamochi version steals travelers’ food and money.
claims.statement_id: Versi Hamochi mencuri makanan dan uang pelancong.
claims.quote: In Hamochi, Sado District (now a part of Sado), it is said that the miage-nyūdō that appears at a place called Tsujidō would steal food and money from travelers.

claims.statement: An Utami account associates it with a stone that changes form.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Utami mengaitkannya dengan batu yang berubah wujud.
claims.quote: In Utami, Ryōtsu (now a part of Sado), it is said that they are in places where trees grow thickly and is dim even at noon, and that a large stone called the "miage-ishi (見上石, look up stone)" has shapeshifted into a nyūdō.

claims.statement: In one account a traveler chanted the "I've seen past you" formula and struck the figure with a rod, and it vanished; after a jizō was deified above the rock, the nyūdō no longer appeared.
claims.statement_id: Menurut satu kisah, seorang pelancong mengucapkan rumus "sudah kulihat tipumu" sambil memukul sosok itu dengan tongkat sehingga ia lenyap; setelah sebuah jizō dipuja di atas batu itu, nyūdō tersebut tidak muncul lagi.
claims.quote: Once, a traveler met this, and by chanting "miage-nyūdō, I've seen past you" and striking it with a rod, the nyūdō disappeared. It is said that afterwards, when a jizō was deified above the rock, the nyūdō no longer appeared.

claims.statement: In a legend from Akadomari, a miage-nyūdō that crushed and killed night travelers fell to the bottom of a ravine, was helped on condition that it no longer attack people and stay away from that place, and no longer appeared there.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda Akadomari, miage-nyūdō yang meremukkan dan membunuh pelancong malam jatuh ke dasar jurang, ditolong dengan syarat tidak menyerang orang lagi dan menjauhi tempat itu, lalu tidak muncul lagi di sana.
claims.quote: Also, in a legend of Akadomari (now a part of Sado), Sado District, there was a miage-nyūdō that squashed and killed night travelers, but it once accidentally fell to the bottom of a ravine, and since it was helped by someone under the condition that it would "no longer attack people" and to "stay away from that place," it no longer appeared there

claims.statement: In Hatano it is said that when someone meeting a miage-nyūdō challenges it by saying the one seen before was much larger, its feet thin out, a violent sound results, and the miage-nyūdō falls down.
claims.statement_id: Di Hatano dikatakan bahwa orang yang bertemu miage-nyūdō dan menantangnya dengan mengatakan bahwa yang dulu dilihatnya jauh lebih besar membuat kakinya mengecil, terdengar bunyi keras, lalu miage-nyūdō itu jatuh.
claims.quote: In Hatano, Sado District (now a part of Sado), it is said that when those who meet a miage-nyūdō say, "the miage-nyūdō I saw before was much larger" and thus challenge it, and since its feet would thus become thinner, a violent sound would result, and the miage-nyūdō would fall down.

claims.statement: Yokai.com lists miage nyūdō among the alternate names of the mikoshi nyūdō, "anticipating priest".
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com mencantumkan miage nyūdō di antara nama lain mikoshi nyūdō, "pendeta yang mengantisipasi".
claims.quote: Mikoshi nyūdō 見越入道 みこしにゅうどう Translation: anticipating priest Alternate names: mikoshi, miage nyūdō, taka bōzu

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, as soon as a person looks up at a mikoshi nyūdō, the giant grows as tall as the observer can raise his eyes, and just as fast.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, begitu orang menengadah pada mikoshi nyūdō, raksasa itu tumbuh setinggi pandangan si pengamat dan secepat itu pula.
claims.quote: As soon as a person raises his eyes to look upon a mikoshi nyūdō, the giant grows to an immense height—as tall the observer is able to raise his eyes, and just as fast.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, looking at a mikoshi nyūdō from its head down to its feet instead of from the feet up saps the giant's power to grow.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, jika orang memandang mikoshi nyūdō dari kepala ke kaki alih-alih dari kaki ke atas, kemampuan raksasa itu untuk bertambah tinggi akan melemah.
claims.quote: Then, look from its head down to its feet, rather than starting at the feet and looking up. If done properly, the giant’s power to grow will be sapped.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, telling the giant that it lost and its trick was anticipated makes it vanish in anger, leaving the traveler to pass safely.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, mengatakan kepada raksasa itu bahwa ia kalah dan tipunya sudah diantisipasi membuatnya lenyap dengan marah sehingga pelancong dapat lewat dengan selamat.
claims.quote: Telling the giant, “You lost! I anticipated your trick!” causes it to vanish in anger, leaving the traveler to pass safely along.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the mikoshi nyūdō form is popular with shape-shifting animals; itachi and tanuki are said to turn into these giants to hunt humans.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, wujud mikoshi nyūdō populer bagi hewan pengubah wujud; itachi dan tanuki disebut berubah menjadi raksasa ini untuk memburu manusia.
claims.quote: Mikoshi nyūdō is a popular form of some shape-shifting animals. In particular, itachi and tanuki transform into these giants in order to hunt humans.

claims.statement: Mikumari denotes a Shinto deity of water distribution.
claims.statement_id: Mikumari menyebut dewa Shinto yang mengatur pembagian air.
claims.quote: 水分神（みくまりのかみ）とは、神道の神。神名の通り、水の分配を司る神で、「くまり」は「配り（くばり）」の意で、水源地や水路の分水点などに祀られる。

claims.statement: The name’s kumari element is explained as distribution.
claims.statement_id: Unsur kumari dalam namanya dijelaskan sebagai pembagian.
claims.quote: 神名の通り、水の分配を司る神で、「くまり」は「配り（くばり）」の意で、水源地や水路の分水点などに祀られる。

claims.statement: Such deities are worshipped at sources and dividing points of waterways.
claims.statement_id: Dewa semacam itu dipuja di sumber dan percabangan saluran air.
claims.quote: 神名の通り、水の分配を司る神で、「くまり」は「配り（くばり）」の意で、水源地や水路の分水点などに祀られる。

claims.statement: Myth identifies heavenly and earthly Mikumari as children of Hayaakitsuhiko and Hayaakitsuhime.
claims.statement_id: Mitos menyebut Mikumari langit dan bumi sebagai anak Hayaakitsuhiko dan Hayaakitsuhime.
claims.quote: 日本神話では、神産みの段でハヤアキツヒコ・ハヤアキツヒメ両神の子として天水分神（あめのみくまりのかみ）・国水分神（くにのみくまりのかみ）が登場する。

claims.statement: Worship includes prayers for rain and links with field and mountain deities.
claims.statement_id: Pemujaannya mencakup doa meminta hujan serta kaitan dengan dewa sawah dan gunung.
claims.quote: 水にかかわる神ということで祈雨の対象ともされ、また、田の神や、水源地に祀られるものは山の神とも結びついた。

claims.statement: A later interpretation connects the deity with children and safe childbirth.
claims.statement_id: Tafsir belakangan menghubungkan dewa itu dengan anak dan persalinan selamat.
claims.quote: 後に、「みくまり」が「みこもり（御子守）」と解され、子供の守護神、子授け・安産の神としても信仰されるようになった。

claims.statement: The Kojiki names both heavenly and earthly Mikumari.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menyebut Mikumari langit dan bumi.
claims.quote: next, Ame no mikumari no kami 天之水分神; next, Kuni no mikumari no kami 国之水分神 (13);

claims.statement: Nakisawame is a goddess in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Nakisawame adalah dewi dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Nakisawame (Japanese: ナキサワメ; recorded in the Kojiki as 泣沢女神 and in the Nihon Shoki as 啼沢女命, sometimes also written as 哭沢女命) is a female kami in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: Her name refers to a weeping female.
claims.statement_id: Namanya merujuk pada perempuan yang menangis.
claims.quote: Her name means "crying weeping female".

claims.statement: Her birth story follows Izanami’s death after bearing the fire deity.
claims.statement_id: Cerita kelahirannya terjadi setelah Izanami meninggal akibat melahirkan dewa api.
claims.quote: During the myth of the Birth of the Gods, in which the goddess Izanami died after giving birth to the fire deity Kagu-tsuchi, Izanagi clung to his wife's dead body and cried.

claims.statement: Nakisawame emerges from Izanagi’s tears.
claims.statement_id: Nakisawame muncul dari air mata Izanagi.
claims.quote: From his tears the deity who lives under the trees on the ridge of Kaguyama 香山 mountain came into existence (16). Its name is Nakisawame no kami 泣沢女神 (17).

claims.statement: She is regarded as a spirit of spring water.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap sebagai roh mata air.
claims.quote: She is considered a spirit of spring water.

claims.statement: A tradition places her at the foot of Mount Kagu.
claims.statement_id: Satu tradisi menempatkannya di kaki Gunung Kagu.
claims.quote: According to the Shinto creation myth, she lives at the foot of Mount Kagu.

claims.statement: Narigama is a yōkai illustrated by Toriyama Sekien.
claims.statement_id: Narigama adalah yōkai yang digambar oleh Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: Narigama (鳴釜; or Narikama, Narukama) or Kamanari (釜鳴) is a Japanese yōkai depicted in Toriyama Sekien's yōkai art collection Gazu Hyakki Tsurezure Bukuro.

claims.statement: Its image wears an iron cooking pot on its head.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya memakai panci besi di kepala.
claims.quote: It is depicted as a hairy figure wearing a kama (iron pot) on its head and holding an ema (votive tablet) in its hand.

claims.statement: The figure holds a votive tablet.
claims.statement_id: Sosok itu memegang papan persembahan.
claims.quote: It is depicted as a hairy figure wearing a kama (iron pot) on its head and holding an ema (votive tablet) in its hand.

claims.statement: Illustrations of the night parade of one hundred demons show it cavorting with other tsukumogami.
claims.statement_id: Ilustrasi parade malam seratus iblis menunjukkannya bersenang-senang bersama tsukumogami lain.
claims.quote: They are often depicted cavorting with other tsukumogami in illustrations of the night parade of one hundred demons.

claims.statement: Its name also refers to divination through the sound of a heated pot.
claims.statement_id: Namanya juga merujuk pada ramalan melalui bunyi panci yang dipanaskan.
claims.quote: The terms Narigama and Kamanari themselves refer to Shinto rituals in which fortune (good or bad luck) is judged based on the sound produced when a pot is heated with fire, or to folk beliefs that view a pot making unexpected sounds as an omen of good or bad luck.

claims.statement: Kibitsu Shrine preserves a sounding-pot ritual.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Kibitsu melestarikan ritual panci berbunyi.
claims.quote: A famous actual example is the Narukama Shinji (Ritual of the Sounding Pot) passed down at Kibitsu Shrine in Okayama Prefecture.

claims.statement: A Japanese dictionary records it as a yōkai that is a monster of a kama (kettle), a kind of tsukumogami, considered to derive from the Narukama Shinji divination ritual of fortune handed down since long ago at Kibitsu Shrine in Okayama Prefecture; it is also called Kamanari (釜鳴).
claims.statement_id: Sebuah kamus Jepang mencatatnya sebagai yōkai berupa makhluk jelmaan kama (ketel), sejenis tsukumogami, yang dianggap berasal dari ritual ramalan untung-rugi "Narukama Shinji" yang sejak lama diwariskan di Kuil Kibitsu, Prefektur Okayama; ia juga disebut Kamanari (釜鳴).
claims.quote: 日本の妖怪。釜の化け物で、付喪神(つくもがみ)の一種。岡山県の吉備津神社に古くから伝わる吉凶占い「鳴釜神事(なるかましんじ)」に由来するものとされる。「釜鳴(かまなり)」とも。

claims.statement: One description presents narigama as tsukumogami of kama, iron kettles or cauldrons used to cook rice in old Japanese kitchens, with long arms and legs.
claims.statement_id: Satu uraian menggambarkan narigama sebagai tsukumogami dari kama, ketel atau kuali besi yang dipakai menanak nasi di dapur Jepang lama, dengan lengan dan tungkai panjang.
claims.quote: Narigama are a tsukumogami of kama, iron kettles or cauldrons used to cook rice in old Japanese kitchens. They have long arms and legs.

claims.statement: According to that account, when the water inside begins to boil, a narigama starts to ring or cry like an animal, and the sound shows whether the weather will be rainy or fair.
claims.statement_id: Menurut uraian itu, saat air di dalamnya mulai mendidih, narigama mulai berdering atau meraung seperti hewan, dan dari bunyinya orang dapat mengetahui apakah cuaca akan hujan atau cerah.
claims.quote: When the water inside begins to boil, a narigama will begin to ring or cry like an animal. Depending on the sound that it emits, it is possible to know whether the weather will be rainy or fair.

claims.statement: According to Sekien, the narigama was first described in the Hakutaku zu, a record of all the supernatural creatures in the world describing their strengths and weaknesses.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Sekien, narigama pertama kali diuraikan dalam Hakutaku zu, catatan semua makhluk gaib di dunia yang menguraikan kekuatan dan kelemahan mereka.
claims.quote: According to Sekien, the narigama was first described in the Hakutaku zu, a record of all the supernatural creatures in the world describing their strengths and weaknesses.

claims.statement: Nigihayahi is a Japanese deity mentioned in several classical chronicles.
claims.statement_id: Nigihayahi adalah dewa Jepang yang disebut dalam beberapa kronik klasik.
claims.quote: Nigihayahi is a Japanese god. He is mentioned in the Kojiki, Kujiki, and Nihon Shoki.

claims.statement: His expedition story ends with killing Nagasunehiko and submitting to Jimmu.
claims.statement_id: Cerita ekspedisinya berakhir dengan membunuh Nagasunehiko dan tunduk kepada Jimmu.
claims.quote: He appears in the legend of Jimmu's Eastern Expedition, killing Nagasunehiko, a follower and the brother-in-law of Nigihayahi, and submitting to Jimmu.

claims.statement: The Mononobe and Hozumi clans regard him as an ancestor.
claims.statement_id: Klan Mononobe dan Hozumi menganggapnya sebagai leluhur.
claims.quote: The Mononobe clan and the Hozumi clan ... state he was their ancestor.

claims.statement: Two chronicles describe his descent in a heavenly rock boat.
claims.statement_id: Dua kronik menggambarkan turunnya dengan perahu batu langit.
claims.quote: According to the Nihongi and Kujiki, Nigihayahi came down from heaven in the "heavenly rock boat," after which he married Mikashigiyahime, Nagasunehiko's younger sister.

claims.statement: Those accounts name Mikashigiyahime as his wife.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah tersebut menyebut Mikashigiyahime sebagai istrinya.
claims.quote: According to the Nihongi and Kujiki, Nigihayahi came down from heaven in the "heavenly rock boat," after which he married Mikashigiyahime, Nagasunehiko's younger sister.

claims.statement: The Kojiki instead uses the wife’s name Tomiyahime.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki justru memakai nama istri Tomiyahime.
claims.quote: In the Kojiki, Nigihayahi marries Tomiyahime instead.

claims.statement: According to the Kokugakuin University Kojiki database synopsis, he came to earth following the descent of the heavenly deity's child, presented the "amatsu-mizu" (天津瑞, heavenly tokens) to Kamuyamato Iwarehiko (Jinmu), who had reached Yamato in the eastern expedition, and served him.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ringkasan basis data Kojiki Universitas Kokugakuin, ia datang ke bumi menyusul turunnya putra dewa langit, lalu mempersembahkan "amatsu-mizu" (天津瑞, pertanda langit) kepada Kamuyamato Iwarehiko (Jinmu) yang telah tiba di Yamato dalam ekspedisi timur dan mengabdi kepadanya.
claims.quote: 天つ神の御子の天降りを追って地上にやってきて、東征で大和に至っていた神倭伊波礼毘古命（神武天皇）に天津瑞を献上してそのもとに仕えた。

claims.statement: In that synopsis he takes as wife Tomiyabime, younger sister of Tomibiko who fought Kamuyamato Iwarehiko; from them was born Umashimaji, ancestor of the Mononobe no Muraji, Hozumi no Omi and Unemeno-omi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam ringkasan itu ia memperistri Tomiyabime, adik Tomibiko yang melawan Kamuyamato Iwarehiko; dari mereka lahir Umashimaji, leluhur Mononobe no Muraji, Hozumi no Omi, dan Unemenoomi.
claims.quote: 神倭伊波礼毘古命と戦った登美毘古の妹である登美夜毘売を妻とし、その間に宇麻志麻遅命（物部連・穂積臣・婇臣らの祖）が生まれている。

claims.statement: In the name, "nigi" is taken as abundant, "haya" as swift and vigorous, and "hi" as spiritual power.
claims.statement_id: Dalam nama itu, "nigi" dipahami sebagai makmur, "haya" sebagai cepat dan bertenaga, dan "hi" sebagai kekuatan rohani.
claims.quote: 神名のニギは「賑」で豊かなさま、ハヤは「速」で勢いの激しいさま、ヒは「霊」で霊力の意とされる。

claims.statement: According to the Nihon Shoki as summarized in that database, Nigihayahi had descended from heaven earlier, married Mikashikiyahime, younger sister of Nagasunehiko, and had a son, Umashimade.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nihon Shoki sebagaimana dirangkum basis data itu, Nigihayahi sudah lebih dulu turun dari langit, menikahi Mikashikiyahime, adik Nagasunehiko, dan mempunyai putra Umashimade.
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』の記事によると、饒速日命は、夙に天から降りて、長髄彦（ながすねびこ）の妹の三炊屋媛（みかしきやひめ）と結婚し、子に可美真手命（うましまでのみこと）を儲けていた。

claims.statement: According to the Nihon Shoki as summarized in that database, Nigihayahi saw Nagasunehiko's perverse nature, killed him, and led his army in submission to Kamuyamato Iwarehiko.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nihon Shoki sebagaimana dirangkum basis data itu, Nigihayahi menilai sifat Nagasunehiko menyimpang, membunuhnya, lalu memimpin pasukannya tunduk kepada Kamuyamato Iwarehiko.
claims.quote: 『日本書紀』の記事によると、饒速日命は、夙に天から降りて、長髄彦（ながすねびこ）の妹の三炊屋媛（みかしきやひめ）と結婚し ... 長髄彦の邪な性質を看取したため、彼を殺し、彼の軍勢を率いて神日本磐余彦尊に帰順した、という。

claims.statement: In the Sendai Kuji Hongi he appears under the name Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Ame no Hoakari Kushitama Nigihayahi no Mikoto; his origin and deeds are identified with those of Ame no Hoakari in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, and he is made a son of Ame no Oshihomimi and elder brother of Ninigi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Sendai Kuji Hongi ia muncul dengan nama Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Ame no Hoakari Kushitama Nigihayahi no Mikoto; asal-usul dan perbuatannya disamakan dengan Ame no Hoakari dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki, dan ia disebut putra Ame no Oshihomimi serta kakak Ninigi.
claims.quote: 『先代旧事本紀』では、「天照国照彦天火明櫛玉饒速日尊」という神名で登場するが、出自や事跡が記紀の天火明命と同一視され、天押穂耳尊の子で瓊々杵尊の兄に当たる神とされている。

claims.statement: The Nigihayahi tradition is often interpreted as reflecting a time when the Mononobe, as rulers of Yamato preceding the emperor, were hostile to him, and as a claim that the Mononobe origin was not inferior to the emperor's.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi Nigihayahi sering ditafsirkan sebagai cerminan masa ketika klan Mononobe, sebagai penguasa Yamato yang mendahului kaisar, memusuhi kaisar, dan sebagai klaim bahwa asal-usul Mononobe tidak lebih rendah dari kaisar.
claims.quote: 邇芸速日命伝承は、物部氏が天皇に先行する大和の支配者としてある時期まで天皇と敵対していた歴史の反映で、物部氏の出自が天皇に劣らないことを主張した伝承と解釈されることが多い。

claims.statement: A counter-view holds that it is merely a clan tradition about descending to help the imperial house, made to raise the clan's standing at court, and should not be seen as reflecting historical fact.
claims.statement_id: Kritik lain menyatakan tradisi itu hanyalah kisah klan tentang turun untuk membantu keluarga kekaisaran dan dibuat untuk mengangkat kedudukan klan di istana, sehingga tidak boleh dipandang sebagai cerminan fakta sejarah.
claims.quote: 一方、飽くまで、天孫降臨神話に見られる諸氏族の始祖神の降臨と同じく、天皇家を助けるために降臨したことを物語った氏族伝承であるとして、天皇との結びつきを示すことで自氏の宮廷内の地位を高めるために成立したに過ぎず、歴史的事実の反映と見るべきではないとする批判もある。

claims.statement: In Aston's translation of the Nihongi, Naga-sune-hiko describes Kushi-dama Nigi-haya-hi no Mikoto as a child of the Heavenly Deity who came down here riding in a Rock-boat of Heaven.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston atas Nihongi, Nagasunehiko menyebut Kushi-dama Nigi-haya-hi no Mikoto sebagai putra Dewa Langit yang turun ke sini menaiki perahu batu langit.
claims.quote: Naga-sune-hiko sent a foot-messenger, who addressed the Emperor, saying: ... Heavenly Deity, who came down from Heaven to dwell here, riding in a Rock-boat of Heaven. His name was Kushi-dama Nigi-haya-hi no Mikoto.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, Nigi-haya-hi took to wife Mi-kashiki-ya-bime, the younger sister of Naga-sune-hiko, who is also called Naga-sune-hime or Tomi-ya-hime, and they had a child, Umashi-ma-te.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, Nigi-haya-hi memperistri adik perempuan Naga-sune-hiko, Mi-kashiki-ya-bime, yang juga disebut Naga-sune-hime atau Tomi-ya-hime, dan mereka mempunyai putra Umashi-ma-te.
claims.quote: Naga-sune-hiko sent a foot-messenger, who addressed the Emperor, saying: ... His name was Kushi-dama Nigi-haya-hi no Mikoto. He took to wife my younger sister ... Mi-kashiki-ya-bime [also called Naga-sune-hime, or Tomi-ya-hime] of whom he at length had a child, named Umashi-ma-te no Mikoto.

claims.statement: In Aston's translation, Nigi-haya-hi knew the Heavenly Deity had bestowed the Empire on the Heavenly Grandchild and judged it useless to instruct Naga-sune, so he put him to death and came with his army to make submission.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston, Nigi-haya-hi mengetahui bahwa Dewa Langit telah menyerahkan kekaisaran kepada Cucu Langit dan menilai Naga-sune tidak dapat diajari, lalu membunuhnya dan datang bersama pasukannya untuk tunduk.
claims.quote: Nigi-haya-hi no Mikoto, knowing from the first that the Heavenly Deity had simply generously bestowed the Empire on the Heavenly Grandchild, and that in view of the perverse disposition of Naga-sune it would be useless to instruct him ... put him to death. He then came with his army and made submission.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, the Emperor praised Nigi-haya-hi and was gracious to him for his faithful service, and he is called the ancestor of the Mono no Be House.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, kaisar memuji dan bersikap ramah kepada Nigi-haya-hi atas pengabdiannya, dan ia disebut leluhur Wangsa Mono no Be.
claims.quote: The Emperor, who from the first had heard that Nigi-haya-hi no Mikoto had come down from Heaven, finding that he now had actually performed faithful service, accordingly praised him, and was gracious to him. He was the ancestor of the Mono no Be House.

claims.statement: Aston's footnote glosses Nigi-haya-hi as "soft-swift-sun".
claims.statement_id: Catatan kaki Aston menerjemahkan Nigi-haya-hi sebagai "matahari lembut-cepat".
claims.quote: Nigi-haya-hi means soft-swift-sun.

claims.statement: Nobusuma is a gliding yōkai associated with Edo.
claims.statement_id: Nobusuma adalah yōkai pelayang yang dikaitkan dengan Edo.
claims.quote: is a type of flying or sky-gliding yōkai monster, whose lore is localized in the Edo (now Tokyo), which some say is a transmuted bat, and others a flying squirrel.

claims.statement: Accounts differ between a transformed bat and a flying squirrel.
claims.statement_id: Kisahnya berbeda antara kelelawar yang berubah dan tupai terbang.
claims.quote: which some say is a transmuted bat, and others a flying squirrel.

claims.statement: It may cover a human’s eyes and mouth.
claims.statement_id: Ia dapat menutupi mata dan mulut manusia.
claims.quote: It may latch onto a human from and cover his eyes and mouth, perhaps to suck blood.

claims.statement: One account includes blood from humans and small animals among its food.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah memasukkan darah manusia dan hewan kecil dalam makanannya.
claims.quote: Nobusuma eat nuts, fruit, and berries, but also feed on fire, and by sucking blood from humans and small animals (such as cats).

claims.statement: Other descriptions include fruit and nuts in its diet.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran lain memasukkan buah dan kacang dalam makanannya.
claims.quote: It is also said to consume fruits or tree-nuts.

claims.statement: A description gives it fire-eating and fire-breathing behavior.
claims.statement_id: Satu gambaran memberinya perilaku memakan dan menyemburkan api.
claims.quote: As for it allegedly consuming flame (or smoke from a fire), a source explains that it engages in a sort of fire-eating and -breathing behavior after chomping the tip off a lit torch.

claims.statement: Nunakawahime is a Shinto goddess and spouse of Ōkuninushi.
claims.statement_id: Nunakawahime adalah dewi Shinto dan istri Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: Nunakawahime (Japanese: 沼河日売 ) is a female Japanese deity (kami) in Shinto and spouse to Ōkuninushi.

claims.statement: Her name is written 沼河日売 in Japanese.
claims.statement_id: Namanya ditulis 沼河日売 dalam bahasa Jepang.
claims.quote: Nunakawahime (Japanese: 沼河日売 ) is a female Japanese deity (kami) in Shinto and spouse to Ōkuninushi.

claims.statement: Ōkuninushi requests marriage through a song.
claims.statement_id: Ōkuninushi melamarnya melalui nyanyian.
claims.quote: When he arrived at her home, he sang a song requesting her hand in marriage.

claims.statement: She replies in song before their marriage the following day.
claims.statement_id: Ia membalas dengan nyanyian sebelum pernikahan mereka keesokan hari.
claims.quote: She returned the song, and the two were married the next day.

claims.statement: According to the Kokugakuin University Kojiki database synopsis, she was a deity of the land of Koshi who was courted by Yachihoko (Ōkuninushi) and became his wife; Yachihoko sent a courtship song to her house, she replied from inside the door, and they married the next night.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ringkasan basis data Kojiki Universitas Kokugakuin, ia adalah dewi dari negeri Koshi yang dilamar Yachihoko (Ōkuninushi) dan menjadi istrinya; Yachihoko mengirim lagu lamaran ke rumahnya, ia membalas dari balik pintu, dan mereka menikah pada malam berikutnya.
claims.quote: 高志国にいた神で、八千矛神（大国主神）に求婚され、その妻となった。八千矛神がその家に到って求婚の歌を贈ると、戸の内から返歌をして、翌日の夜に結婚した。

claims.statement: In the name Nunakawa, "nu" is taken to mean jewel, so Nunakawa is thought to mean a river that produces jewels.
claims.statement_id: Dalam nama Nunakawa, "nu" dipahami sebagai permata, sehingga Nunakawa dianggap berarti sungai penghasil permata.
claims.quote: ヌナカハのヌは玉の意とされ、 ... ヌナカハとは、玉を産出する川の意と考えられている（ナは連体助詞）。

claims.statement: Because the Nunakawa district is a source of jade, some interpretations see Nunakawahime as chief of the jewel-making group there or as a queen controlling the jade of Koshi.
claims.statement_id: Karena Nunakawa-gō adalah daerah asal batu giok, ada tafsir yang memandang Nunakawahime sebagai kepala kelompok pembuat permata di sana atau ratu yang menguasai giok negeri Koshi.
claims.quote: 翡翠の原産地という沼川郷の地理的な特質から、沼河比売の性格は、その地の玉作り集団の首長とする説や、越国の翡翠を支配する女王と捉える説がある。

claims.statement: The Kojiki records no descendants, but the later Sendai Kuji Hongi records an alternate tradition that she bore Takeminakata, deity of Suwa Shrine, to Ōkuninushi.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki tidak mencatat keturunannya, tetapi Sendai Kuji Hongi yang lebih muda mencatat versi lain bahwa ia melahirkan Takeminakata, dewa Kuil Suwa, dari Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: なお、『古事記』には子孫の記述がないが、時代の降る『先代旧事本紀』には、沼河比売が大国主神との間に、諏訪神社の祭神、建御名方神を生んだという異伝が記されている。

claims.statement: In the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki, entry for Mihogō in Shimane District, the great god who made the world married Nunagiwahime, grandchild of the Koshi deity Okitsukushii, and bore Mihosusumi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Izumo no Kuni Fudoki, bagian Mihogō, Distrik Shimane, sang dewa pencipta dunia menikahi Nunagiwahime, cucu dewa Okitsukushii dari negeri Koshi, dan melahirkan Mihosusumi.
claims.quote: 『出雲国風土記』島根郡美保郷の条には、天の下造らしし大神の命が、高志の国に坐す神「意支都久辰為（おきつくしゐ）命」の子「俾都久辰為（へつくしゐ）命」の子「奴奈宜波比売（ぬながはひめ）命」と婚して「御穂須々美（みほすすみ）命」を生んだとある。

claims.statement: Koshi (Koshi no kuni), where Nunakawahime lived, is the pre-division name of a wide Hokuriku area covering Echizen, Etchū and Echigo.
claims.statement_id: Koshi (Koshi no kuni) tempat Nunakawahime tinggal adalah nama lama wilayah Hokuriku yang luas sebelum dibagi menjadi Echizen, Etchū, dan Echigo.
claims.quote: 沼河比売が居た「高志国」（越国）は、北陸地方の広域にわたる、越前・越中・越後の分割前の国名である。

claims.statement: Around present-day Itoigawa, shrines bearing the name Nunakawa and shrines enshrining Nunakawahime are spread widely, and various traditions about her are still handed down.
claims.statement_id: Di sekitar Itoigawa sekarang, kuil bernama Nunakawa dan kuil yang memuja Nunakawahime tersebar di banyak tempat, dan berbagai tradisi tentangnya masih diwariskan.
claims.quote: 現・糸魚川市あたりには、ヌナカハとつく神社や沼河比売を祭る神社が随所に分布し、沼河比売にまつわる伝承も今日まで様々伝わっている。

claims.statement: The story of an Izumo deity marrying Nunakawahime of Koshi is regarded as based on a regional connection between ancient Izumo and Koshi.
claims.statement_id: Kisah dewa Izumo yang menikahi Nunakawahime dari Koshi dianggap berlandaskan hubungan kewilayahan Izumo kuno dengan Koshi.
claims.quote: 『古事記』『出雲国風土記』の沼河比売の神話で、出雲の神が越の沼河比売と結婚するという内容は、古代の出雲と越との間に地域的な結びつきがあったことが基盤になっているとされる。

claims.statement: Because the names of Nunagiwahime's ancestral deities, Okitsu and Hetsu, mean "of the offing" and "of the seashore" and are thought to be sea deities, some interpretations see her as a daughter of a sea deity.
claims.statement_id: Karena nama leluhur Nunagiwahime, Okitsu dan Hetsu, berarti "di laut" dan "di tepi laut" dan dianggap dewa laut, ada tafsir yang memandangnya putri dewa laut.
claims.quote: 奴奈宜波比売命の祖神の神名のオキツ・ヘツは「沖の」「海辺の」の意で、海神と考えられ、これによって沼河比売を海神の娘と捉える説もある。

claims.statement: Okuri-suzume is a yōkai known in Wakayama Prefecture and in Higashiyoshino Village, Yoshino District, Nara Prefecture.
claims.statement_id: Okuri-suzume adalah yōkai yang dikisahkan di Prefektur Wakayama dan di Desa Higashiyoshino, Distrik Yoshino, Prefektur Nara.
claims.quote: 送り雀（おくりすずめ）は、和歌山県や奈良県吉野郡東吉野村に伝わる妖怪。和歌山では雀送り（すずめおくり）ともいう。

claims.statement: Wakayama also uses the name suzume-okuri.
claims.statement_id: Wakayama juga memakai nama suzume-okuri.
claims.quote: 和歌山では雀送り（すずめおくり）ともいう。その鳴き声を実在の鳥のアオジにたとえ、蒿雀（あおじ）とも呼ばれる。

claims.statement: It approaches people walking mountain paths at night while calling.
claims.statement_id: Ia mendekati orang yang berjalan di jalur pegunungan malam hari sambil bersuara.
claims.quote: 夜、人が山道を歩いていると「チチチチ……」と鳴きながら飛んでくる。夜に提灯を灯して歩いていると、寄って来るともいう。

claims.statement: Its call is said to precede wolves or an okuri-ōkami.
claims.statement_id: Suaranya konon mendahului serigala atau okuri-ōkami.
claims.quote: この鳴き声の後にはオオカミ、もしくは妖怪・送り狼が現れるといい、道で転倒するとすぐにそれらに襲撃されてしまうため、送り雀の鳴き声を聞いた者は、転ばないよう足元に注意を払いつつ歩いたという。

claims.statement: As the name suggests it is said to be bird-shaped, yet no one has seen its form; some say its true identity is the aoji (a real bird), others note it flies at night and so differs from the aoji, and in some regions it is said to be a hare.
claims.statement_id: Sesuai namanya ia dianggap berwujud burung, tetapi tak seorang pun pernah melihat wujudnya; ada yang menyebut wujud aslinya aoji (burung nyata), ada yang menunjuk bahwa ia terbang malam sehingga berbeda dari aoji, dan di sebagian daerah dikatakan sebenarnya kelinci.
claims.quote: 雀の名の通り、鳥の姿だとされるが、その姿を見た者は誰もいない。前述のアオジが送り雀の正体ともいうが、夜に飛ぶためにアオジとは違うとの指摘もあり、実は兎だという地域もある。

claims.statement: A similar yōkai is the yosuzume ("night sparrow"); in Nara the yosuzume is sometimes identified with the okuri-suzume.
claims.statement_id: Yōkai serupa adalah yosuzume ("burung pipit malam"); di Nara, yosuzume kadang disamakan dengan okuri-suzume.
claims.quote: また、これと似た妖怪に「夜雀」があり、奈良では夜雀が送り雀と同一視されることもある。

claims.statement: It is also said to come near when someone walks at night carrying a lantern, and in Wakayama it often appeared on Mount Myōhō.
claims.statement_id: Dikatakan ia mendekat ketika orang berjalan dengan lentera di malam hari, dan di Wakayama sering muncul di Gunung Myōhō.
claims.quote: 夜に提灯を灯して歩いていると、寄って来るともいう。和歌山では妙法山によく現れたという。

claims.statement: A summary in the Nichibunken yōkai tradition database for a case in Nara Prefecture (Gojō, Ōto) says there was a "night sparrow" that chirped "chitchi, chitchi" at night and followed people, and the teller had heard it called okuri-suzume.
claims.statement_id: Ringkasan dalam basis data tradisi yōkai Nichibunken untuk kasus di Prefektur Nara (Gojō, Ōto) menyebut ada "yosuzume" yang berkicau "chitchi, chitchi" di malam hari dan mengikuti orang, dan si pencerita pernah mendengar itu disebut okuri-suzume.
claims.quote: 地域（都道府県名） 奈良県 ■ 地域（市・郡名） 五條市 ■ 地域（区町村名） 大塔町 ■ 要約 夜雀というのがいた。夜に、ちっち、ちっちと鳴き、ついて来た。それが送り雀だということを聞いたことがある。

claims.statement: One summary in the Nichibunken database says the okuri-suzume follows at dusk chirping "chinchin" but does no harm.
claims.statement_id: Satu ringkasan dalam basis data Nichibunken menyebut okuri-suzume mengikuti sambil berkicau "chinchin" menjelang malam tetapi tidak berbuat jahat.
claims.quote: 晩方、送り雀がチンチンと鳴き声をさせてついてくるが、悪いことはしない。

claims.statement: One summary in the Nichibunken database says the okuri-suzume flies back and forth on night mountain paths chirping, but since it flies at night it is said not to be a bird; its call is said to signal that an okuri-ōkami is following.
claims.statement_id: Satu ringkasan dalam basis data Nichibunken menyebut okuri-suzume terbang bolak-balik di jalan gunung malam hari sambil berkicau, tetapi karena terbang malam ia disebut bukan burung; kicauannya dikatakan pertanda okuri-ōkami (serigala pengantar) ada di dekat.
claims.quote: オクリスズメは夜の山道でちちちちと啼きながら後先を飛ぶ小鳥であるといわれているが、夜に飛ぶので鳥ではない。送雀が鳴くと送狼がついているしらせだといわれる。

claims.statement: One summary in the Nichibunken database says someone walking at night with a lantern hears chirping "chi, chi, chi" but no one has seen its form; some say a hare, others the aoji, and it is thought not to be a bird.
claims.statement_id: Satu ringkasan dalam basis data Nichibunken menyebut orang berjalan malam dengan lentera mendengar kicauan "chi, chi, chi" tetapi tak seorang pun melihat wujudnya; ada yang bilang kelinci, ada yang bilang aoji, dan ada yang menganggapnya bukan burung.
claims.quote: 夜、提灯を持って歩くと、チ、チ、チ、と送雀の鳴き声がきこえるが、その姿を見た人はいない。兎だともいう。又、あおじだという人もいるが、鳥ではないらしい。

claims.statement: One summary in the Nichibunken database says the okuri-suzume follows chirping as one walks a mountain path at night, no one has seen its form, and when it follows, wolves are said to follow too.
claims.statement_id: Satu ringkasan dalam basis data Nichibunken menyebut okuri-suzume mengikuti sambil berkicau saat orang berjalan di jalan gunung malam, tak seorang pun melihat wujudnya, dan bila ia mengikuti, serigala ikut mengikuti.
claims.quote: 送り雀は夜に山道を歩いているとチンチンと鳴きながらあとをつけてくるが、誰も姿を見たことはない。送り雀がついてくると、狼も一緒についてくるといわれている。

claims.statement: Omizunu is a Japanese deity in the Izumo Fudoki.
claims.statement_id: Omizunu adalah dewa Jepang dalam Izumo Fudoki.
claims.quote: Omizunu (Japanese: 淤美豆奴神 , Hepburn: Omizunu no Kami) is a Japanese deity (kami) who appears in the Izumo Fudoki where he expands Izumo Province.

claims.statement: The narrative has him expand Izumo Province.
claims.statement_id: Narasi menyebutnya memperluas Provinsi Izumo.
claims.quote: Omizunu (Japanese: 淤美豆奴神 , Hepburn: Omizunu no Kami) is a Japanese deity (kami) who appears in the Izumo Fudoki where he expands Izumo Province.

claims.statement: His genealogy traces descent from Susanoo.
claims.statement_id: Silsilahnya menelusuri keturunan Susanoo.
claims.quote: He is descended from Susanoo, is son of Fukabuchi-no-Mizuyarehana and Ame-no-Tsudohechine, and married to Futemimi with whom he sires Ame-no-Fuyukinu.

claims.statement: He and Futemimi are parents of Ame-no-Fuyukinu.
claims.statement_id: Ia dan Futemimi adalah orang tua Ame-no-Fuyukinu.
claims.quote: He is descended from Susanoo, is son of Fukabuchi-no-Mizuyarehana and Ame-no-Tsudohechine, and married to Futemimi with whom he sires Ame-no-Fuyukinu.

claims.statement: According to the Kokugakuin University Kojiki database synopsis, he appears in the genealogy of Susanoo: a deity born when Fukabuchi-no-Mizuyarehana married Ame-no-Tsudohechine, and he married Futemimi, daughter of Funozunu, and begot Ame-no-Fuyukinu.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ringkasan basis data Kojiki Universitas Kokugakuin, ia muncul dalam silsilah Susanoo: dewa yang lahir dari Fukabuchi-no-Mizuyarehana yang menikahi Ame-no-Tsudohechine, dan ia menikahi Futemimi, putri Funozunu, lalu melahirkan Ame-no-Fuyukinu.
claims.quote: 須佐之男命の系譜中に見える。深淵之水夜礼花神が天之都度閉知泥神を娶って生んだ神。布怒豆怒神の娘の布帝耳神を娶って、天之冬衣神を生んだ。

claims.statement: Because he belongs to a lineage of water-related deities, his name is explained through water, and one view takes it to mean "great water lord".
claims.statement_id: Karena ia termasuk silsilah dewa yang berkaitan dengan air, namanya dijelaskan lewat air, dan ada tafsir yang memahaminya sebagai "penguasa air besar".
claims.quote: 淤美豆奴神は、水にちなむ神の系譜に連なっているから、名義も水に関連して説かれ、大水主の意かとする説がある。

claims.statement: The related deity in the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki, Yatsukamizu-omitsuno no Mikoto or Omizuno no Mikoto, is the protagonist of the Kunibiki (land-pulling) myth, was worshipped chiefly in Shimane District, and ranks next below the supreme god Ōanamochi.
claims.statement_id: Dewa terkait dalam Izumo no Kuni Fudoki, Yatsukamizu-omitsuno no Mikoto atau Omizuno no Mikoto, adalah tokoh utama mitos Kunibiki (menarik daratan), dipuja terutama di Distrik Shimane, dan menempati kedudukan tepat di bawah dewa tertinggi Ōanamochi.
claims.quote: 関連が説かれている『出雲国風土記』の八束水臣津野命・意美豆努命は、国引き神話の主人公である。この神は、島根郡を中心に信仰された神と把握され、風土記中では「国引き坐しし」神として国土の創造神に位置付けられる事跡が語られており、最高神の「天の下造りましし大神」大穴持命に次ぐ地位を占めている。

claims.statement: If the two deities are regarded as the same, the Fudoki recounts major deeds while the Kojiki gives only the name; one view suggests the deeds were absorbed into Ōkuninushi.
claims.statement_id: Jika kedua dewa dianggap sama, Fudoki menceritakan perbuatan penting, sedangkan Kojiki hanya menyebut nama; satu tafsir menduga perbuatan itu diserap oleh Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: これら『古事記』と『出雲国風土記』との神を同神とみると、両書の関係についても問題となる。風土記ではその伝承において重大な事跡が語られているのに対して、『古事記』では名前が挙がるだけでその事跡には触れられていない。この理由について、『古事記』ではその事跡が大国主神に吸収されたためではないかとする説がある。

claims.statement: For Omitsuno in the Fudoki, views agree it means "great water lord", while the preceding "Yatsukamizu" has been interpreted in various ways.
claims.statement_id: Untuk Omitsuno dalam Fudoki, tafsir sepakat artinya "penguasa air besar", sedangkan "Yatsukamizu" yang menyertainya ditafsirkan dengan banyak cara.
claims.quote: 「臣津野」は大水主の意として諸説一致しているが、その修飾語となる「八束水」について様々な見解が提示されている。

claims.statement: Rashōmon no oni is an ogre associated with the gate of Heian-kyō.
claims.statement_id: Rashōmon no oni adalah oni yang dikaitkan dengan gerbang Heian-kyō.
claims.quote: Rashōmon no oni (羅城門の鬼 or 羅生門の鬼) is an oni said to have nested at the front gate of Heian-kyō, Rashōmon.

claims.statement: Watanabe no Tsuna rides out alone to investigate the gate.
claims.statement_id: Watanabe no Tsuna berkuda sendirian untuk memeriksa gerbang.
claims.quote: One of the Shitennō, Watanabe no Tsuna, said there was no logical basis for an oni to dwell on royal grounds, so in order to go check, he armed himself with armor, a helmet, and his ancestral tachi and rode out on a horse all by himself to Rashōmon without any accompany followers.

claims.statement: A sudden wind stops his horse near the gate.
claims.statement_id: Angin mendadak menghentikan kudanya dekat gerbang.
claims.quote: Upon coming to the main road Kujō-doori with the front side of Rashōmon coming into view, there was a gust of sudden wind, and the horse stopped moving.

claims.statement: The oni appears behind him and grabs his helmet.
claims.statement_id: Oni muncul dari belakang dan meraih helmnya.
claims.quote: As Tsuna disembarked from his horse and headed towards Rashōmon, an oni appeared from behind him and caught his helmet.

claims.statement: Tsuna strikes at it but loses his helmet.
claims.statement_id: Tsuna menyerangnya tetapi kehilangan helmnya.
claims.quote: Tsuna cut at it with his tachi without delay, but his helmet was stolen.

claims.statement: Their duel ends with Tsuna cutting off the oni’s arm.
claims.statement_id: Duel mereka berakhir dengan Tsuna memotong lengan oni.
claims.quote: Tsuna's tachi and the oni's iron rod clashed violent, until finally, Tsuna cut off one of the oni's arm.

claims.statement: In The Tale of the Heike (Tsurugi no Maki), the story of the oni at Itijō Modoribashi happens at a bridge called Ichijō Modoribashi, and afterward the oni disguised itself as Tsuna's mother and stole the arm.
claims.statement_id: Dalam The Tale of the Heike (bagian Tsurugi no Maki), kisah oni di Itijō Modoribashi terjadi di jembatan bernama Ichijō Modoribashi, dan sesudahnya oni itu menyamar sebagai ibu Tsuna lalu mencuri kembali lengannya.
claims.quote: In The Tale of the Heike, Tsurugi no Maki, the story about the oni at Itijō Modoribashi happens at a bridge called Ichijō Modoribashi, and afterward, the oni disguised itself as Tsuna's mother and stole the arm.

claims.statement: Because of this, the different oni of Rashōmon is often viewed as the same as Ibaraki-dōji.
claims.statement_id: Karena itu, oni Rashōmon yang berbeda sering dipandang sama dengan Ibaraki-dōji.
claims.quote: Because of this, the different oni, the oni of Rashōmon, is often viewed to be the same as Ibaraki-dōji.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Rashōmon was built in 789 but after the Heian period fell into serious disrepair and became known as an unsavory place.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, Rashōmon dibangun pada 789 tetapi setelah zaman Heian rusak parah dan dikenal sebagai tempat yang tidak menyenangkan.
claims.quote: Rashōmon was built in 789, but after the Heian period it fell into serious disrepair and became known as an unsavory place.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, an enormous hand suddenly reached out of the dark to grab Tsuna's helmet, and Tsuna severed the arm of an enormous demon; it was Ibaraki dōji, coming to avenge the murder of Shuten dōji.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, sebuah tangan raksasa tiba-tiba menjulur dari kegelapan merebut helm Tsuna, lalu Tsuna menebas lengan iblis raksasa itu; iblis itu adalah Ibaraki dōji yang datang membalas kematian Shuten dōji.
claims.quote: Approaching the gate in the fierce gale, he noticed an enormous hand suddenly reach out of the dark to grab his helmet. Tsuna wasted no time, and swung his great katana around, severing the arm of an enormous demon: it was Ibaraki dōji, coming to avenge the murder of Shuten dōji.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Ibaraki dōji later returned to Rashōmon looking for her arm; she disguised herself as Watanabe no Tsuna's wet nurse, stole back her severed arm, and fled.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, Ibaraki dōji kembali ke Rashōmon mencari lengannya; ia menyamar sebagai ibu susu Watanabe no Tsuna, mencuri kembali lengannya, dan kabur.
claims.quote: Ibaraki dōji later returned to Rashōmon, looking for her arm. She disguised herself as Watanabe no Tsuna’s wetnurse, and was able to steal back her severed arm and flee.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the injured demon ran away leaving her arm behind, and Rashōmon was no longer haunted.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, iblis yang terluka lari meninggalkan lengannya, dan Rashōmon tidak lagi angker.
claims.quote: The injured demon ran away, leaving her arm behind, and Rashōmon was no longer haunted.

claims.statement: Onihitokuchi names legends of oni eating humans in one mouthful.
claims.statement_id: Onihitokuchi menyebut legenda oni yang memakan manusia dalam sekali lahap.
claims.quote: Onihitokuchi (鬼一口) refers to a Japanese setsuwa (legend) in which oni (ogres) eat humans in one mouthful.

claims.statement: The expression also signifies extreme danger or swift handling.
claims.statement_id: Ungkapan itu juga menandakan bahaya besar atau penanganan cepat.
claims.quote: This in turn refers to something extremely dangerous and difficult, as well as the quick and easy handling of things.

claims.statement: One tale places a fleeing woman in a cellar during a storm.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita menempatkan perempuan yang melarikan diri di gudang bawah tanah saat badai.
claims.quote: One time, the man finally stole that woman, but while he was fleeing, as the night grew late, a thunderstorm came, so he found a cellar that did not fasten its doors and made the woman go in, and with a bow and arrow in his own possession, stood guard in front of the cellar, and waited for dawn.

claims.statement: At dawn, her companion finds her missing.
claims.statement_id: Saat fajar, pendampingnya mendapati perempuan itu hilang.
claims.quote: Before long, dawn came and when he peeped into the cellar, there was no figure of any woman.

claims.statement: The story says a cellar-dwelling oni ate her.
claims.statement_id: Cerita menyebut oni penghuni gudang memakannya.
claims.quote: The woman was killed and eaten in one mouthful by an oni that lived in the cellar, and the shriek that she made when she died was erased by the sound of lightning.

claims.statement: A reference associates the story’s origins with the Heian period.
claims.statement_id: Satu rujukan mengaitkan asal cerita dengan zaman Heian.
claims.quote: A famous example of oni hitokuchi appears in the Heian Period story collection Ise monogatari .

claims.statement: Osakabehime is a yōkai associated with Himeji Castle.
claims.statement_id: Osakabehime adalah yōkai yang dikaitkan dengan Kastel Himeji.
claims.quote: She is described as a yōkai inhabiting Himeji Castle.

claims.statement: She lives in the tower and meets the lord once each year.
claims.statement_id: Ia tinggal di menara dan menemui penguasa kastel sekali setahun.
claims.quote: Osakabehime lives in the castle tower of Himeji Castle, and meets the castle lord only once a year to tell him the fate of the castle.

claims.statement: She announces the castle’s fate at that meeting.
claims.statement_id: Ia mengumumkan nasib kastel dalam pertemuan tersebut.
claims.quote: Osakabehime lives in the castle tower of Himeji Castle, and meets the castle lord only once a year to tell him the fate of the castle.

claims.statement: An essay explains her seclusion as dislike of people.
claims.statement_id: Satu esai menjelaskan penyendiriannya sebagai ketidaksukaan kepada manusia.
claims.quote: According to Matsuura Shizuyama's essay Kasshi Yawa, the reason why Osakabehime lives in hiding like this is because she hates people.

claims.statement: Early stories use both male and female forms.
claims.statement_id: Cerita awal memakai wujud laki-laki maupun perempuan.
claims.quote: Gender of this yōkai was not clearly determined in Shokokuhyakumonogatari (appeared in various forms including men and women), but eventually they came to be considered a woman.

claims.statement: One interpretation connects the later princess title with Himeji.
claims.statement_id: Satu tafsir menghubungkan gelar putri belakangan dengan Himeji.
claims.quote: It is believed that this was related Osakabe becoming Osakabehime (Princess Osakabe), "-hime" coming from Himeji.

claims.statement: Osakabehime (刑部姫) is a figure in Japanese folklore described as a yōkai inhabiting Himeji Castle; a Kabuki play based on her story is considered one of the Shin-Kabuki Jūhachiban.
claims.statement_id: Osakabehime (刑部姫) adalah tokoh cerita rakyat Jepang yang digambarkan sebagai yōkai penghuni Kastil Himeji; sebuah lakon Kabuki berdasarkan kisahnya dianggap salah satu Shin-Kabuki Jūhachiban.
claims.quote: Osakabehime (刑部姫) is a figure in Japanese folklore. She is described as a yōkai inhabiting Himeji Castle. A Kabuki play based on her story is considered one of the Shin-Kabuki Jūhachiban.

claims.statement: In early legends and works such as the Shokokuhyakumonogatari (1677), the yōkai was just called "Castle Monster" (城ばけ物).
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda dan karya awal seperti Shokokuhyakumonogatari (1677), yōkai ini hanya disebut "Castle Monster" (城ばけ物).
claims.quote: However, in early legends and creations such as Shokokuhyakumonogatari (諸国百物語, 1677), the yōkai was just called "Castle Monster" (城ばけ物).

claims.statement: Toyotomi Hideyoshi removed the shrine and re-enshrined Osakabe in Harima Sōja, a shrine dedicated to several gods on the outskirts of the town, when the castle was expanded.
claims.statement_id: Toyotomi Hideyoshi memindahkan kuil dan mengabadikan kembali Osakabe di Harima Sōja, kuil bagi beberapa dewa di pinggiran kota, ketika kastil diperluas.
claims.quote: Toyotomi Hideyoshi removed the shrine and re-enshrined Osakabe in Harima Sōja, a shrine dedicated to several gods to the outskirts of the town when the castle was expanded.

claims.statement: After the new castle tower was completed in 1608 various mysteries occurred, and in 1611 Terumasa fell ill; rumors held it was a curse of the god Osakabe, so the Ikeda family built a shrine in the castle and relocated the god.
claims.statement_id: Setelah menara kastil baru selesai pada 1608 terjadi berbagai keanehan, dan pada 1611 Terumasa jatuh sakit; muncul kabar bahwa itu kutukan dewa Osakabe, sehingga keluarga Ikeda membangun kuil di dalam kastil dan memindahkan dewa itu.
claims.quote: when the new castle tower was completed in 1608, various mysteries occurred, and in 1611 Terumasa finally fell ill. Rumors circulated that this was a curse of the god Osakabe, so the Ikeda family built a shrine in the castle and relocated the god.

claims.statement: Yokai.com writes her name as 長壁姫 and translates it "the lady of the walls"; her habitat is the secret areas of Himeji Castle.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis namanya 長壁姫 dan menerjemahkannya "the lady of the walls"; habitatnya adalah area rahasia di Kastil Himeji.
claims.quote: Osakabe hime 長壁姫 おさかべひめ Translation: the lady of the walls Habitat: secret areas of Himeji Castle

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, she is a powerful yōkai able to manipulate people like puppets, extremely knowledgeable, and in control of a multitude of kenzokushin, animal-like spirits who act as messengers.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ia yōkai yang kuat, mampu menggerakkan orang seperti boneka, sangat berpengetahuan, dan mengendalikan banyak kenzokushin, roh mirip hewan yang menjadi pesuruh.
claims.quote: Osakabe hime is a powerful yōkai, capable of manipulating people like puppets. She is extremely knowledgeable about many things and controls a multitude of kenzokushin—animal-like spirits who act as messengers.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, she can read a person's heart and see their true desires and then manipulate them as she pleases; it is rumored that anyone who sees her face dies instantly.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ia dapat membaca hati dan melihat keinginan sejati seseorang lalu memanipulasinya sesukanya; dikabarkan siapa pun yang melihat wajahnya langsung mati.
claims.quote: She can read a person’s heart and see their true desires. She can then manipulate them any way she pleases. It is rumored that anybody who sees her face will die instantly.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, she takes the appearance of a majestic old woman wearing a 12-layered kimono.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ia berwujud perempuan tua yang agung mengenakan kimono dua belas lapis.
claims.quote: She takes the appearance of a majestic old woman wearing a 12-layered kimono.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, by popular account she is actually an elderly nine-tailed kitsune; other accounts say she may be a snake spirit or the ghost of one of Emperor Fushimi's favorite courtesans.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, menurut kisah populer ia sebenarnya kitsune berekor sembilan yang sudah tua; kisah lain menyebutnya roh ular atau hantu salah satu selir kesayangan Kaisar Fushimi.
claims.quote: By popular account, she is actually an elderly nine-tailed kitsune who takes the form of this yōkai. According to other accounts, she may be a snake spirit, or the ghost of one of Emperor Fushimi’s favorite courtesans.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, another common legend says she was originally the kami of the mountain upon which Himeji Castle was built.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, legenda umum lain menyebut ia semula kami gunung tempat Kastil Himeji dibangun.
claims.quote: Another common legend is that she was originally the kami of the mountain upon which Himeji Castle was built.

claims.statement: Osaki is a yōkai in Japanese legends.
claims.statement_id: Osaki adalah yōkai dalam legenda Jepang.
claims.quote: Osaki is a type of yokai told about in legends of Japan.

claims.statement: It is also known as osaki-gitsune.
claims.statement_id: Ia juga dikenal sebagai osaki-gitsune.
claims.quote: They are also called osaki-gitsune.

claims.statement: Its name has several written forms.
claims.statement_id: Namanya memiliki beberapa bentuk penulisan.
claims.quote: Other ways of writing them include 尾裂, 御先狐, 尾崎狐, among others.

claims.statement: Its traditions occur in mountain villages of Kantō and nearby areas.
claims.statement_id: Tradisinya terdapat di desa pegunungan Kantō dan wilayah sekitar.
claims.quote: They are in the folk beliefs of certain mountain villages of the Kantō region as well as other areas such as the Saitama Prefecture, the Okutama region of Tokyo Metropolis, the Gunma Prefecture, the Tochigi Prefecture, the Ibaraki Prefecture, the Nagano Prefecture, among other regions.

claims.statement: A legend explains its absence from Edo through a river boundary or Inari protection.
claims.statement_id: Satu legenda menjelaskan ketidakhadirannya di Edo melalui batas sungai atau perlindungan Inari.
claims.quote: There are no legends of this in Tokyo other than in Tama, and this said to be because osaki are unable to cross the Toda river (a part of Warabi-shuku) or because in Kantō Hasshū (eight Edo provinces of Kantō), there was the head of the foxes, the Ōji Inari Jinja, preventing the osaki from entering Edo.

claims.statement: Several explanations link its name with fox tails or divine attendants.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa penjelasan menghubungkan namanya dengan ekor rubah atau pengiring dewa.
claims.quote: Its name is said to come from how it was born from one of the nine-tailed fox's tails, so it was called "osaki" (尾先, "tail-front"), and according to the Toen Shōsetsu (兎園小説) by Kyokutei Bakin and others, the tail split into two, which is why it is "osaki" (尾裂, "tail-split"), and there is also the theory that its name comes from misaki, meaning kin of gods.

claims.statement: Yokai.com writes the name as オサキ, lists osaki gitsune ("osaki fox") as an alternate name, and gives its habitat as forests and mountains, also found in homes and human bodies.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis namanya オサキ, mencantumkan osaki gitsune ("rubah osaki") sebagai nama lain, dan menyebut habitatnya hutan dan gunung, serta ditemukan di rumah dan tubuh manusia.
claims.quote: Osaki オサキ おさき Translation: varies depending on the kanji used Alternate names: osaki gitsune (“osaki fox”) Habitat: forests and mountains; also found in homes and human bodies

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, osaki are small, magical mammals with fluffy tails that split at the end, resembling weasels or mice, or very small foxes.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, osaki adalah mamalia kecil bersifat gaib dengan ekor berbulu yang ujungnya terbelah, mirip musang atau tikus, atau rubah yang sangat kecil.
claims.quote: Osaki are small, magical mammals with fluffy tails that split at the end. They resemble weasels or mice, or very small foxes.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, osaki are usually invisible to the human eye but show themselves at the sound of a pot lid or rice container being struck, and are extremely fast so they appear and disappear suddenly.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, osaki biasanya tak terlihat mata manusia tetapi menampakkan diri saat tutup panci atau wadah nasi dipukul, dan sangat cepat sehingga muncul dan lenyap tiba-tiba.
claims.quote: They are usually invisible to the human eye, but will show themselves at the sound of a pot lid or a rice container being struck. They are extremely fast, so they appear and disappear suddenly.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, if kept happy, osaki are able to bring material wealth to their owners and ruin to their owners' enemies.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, jika dijaga agar senang, osaki dapat membawa kekayaan bagi pemiliknya dan kehancuran bagi musuh pemiliknya.
claims.quote: If kept happy, osaki are able to bring material wealth to their owners and ruin to their owners’ enemies.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, like other kinds of kitsune, osaki can enter human bodies; this power, called kitsune tsuki, is used against people who have wronged the osaki or its human family.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, seperti jenis kitsune lain, osaki dapat memasuki tubuh manusia; kekuatan yang disebut kitsune tsuki ini dipakai terhadap orang yang berbuat salah kepada osaki atau keluarga manusianya.
claims.quote: Like other kinds of kitsune, osaki are capable of entering human bodies. This power is called kitsune tsuki, and is used against people who have wronged the osaki or its human family.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, victims of osaki possession are struck with bad luck and mysterious injuries, fevers, agitation, gluttonous appetites and other eccentricities; the possession can only be cured through difficult exorcisms.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, korban perasukan osaki tertimpa nasib buruk dan cedera misterius, demam, gelisah, nafsu makan rakus, dan keanehan lain; perasukan itu hanya dapat disembuhkan lewat pengusiran roh yang sulit.
claims.quote: Victims of osaki possession are struck with bad luck and mysterious injuries. They develop fevers, mental and physical agitation, gluttonous appetites, and other eccentricities. This possession can only be cured through difficult exorcisms.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, osaki are said to come from the nine-tailed kitsune Tamamo no Mae: when she was killed her body became the cursed stone Sesshō seki, which the priest Gennō smashed; pieces of her tails landed in Gunma and became the first osaki.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, osaki dikatakan berasal dari kitsune berekor sembilan Tamamo no Mae: setelah ia dibunuh tubuhnya menjadi batu terkutuk Sesshō seki, yang dipecahkan oleh pendeta Gennō; sebagian pecahan ekor Tamamo no Mae jatuh di Gunma dan menjadi osaki pertama.
claims.quote: Osaki are said to come from the great nine-tailed kitsune Tamamo no Mae. When she was killed, her body transformed into a great cursed stone called Sesshō seki. Its curse was ended when the priest Gennō smashed the rock into pieces, which then flew across the country. Some of the pieces of Tamamo no Mae’s tails landed in Gunma and transformed into the first osaki.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, villagers are cautioned not to tease wild osaki in order to avoid invoking their curse.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, penduduk desa diperingatkan agar tidak mengusik osaki liar supaya tidak memicu kutukannya.
claims.quote: Villagers are cautioned not to tease wild osaki in order to avoid invoking their curse.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, osaki mochi families were historically shunned and mistrusted for their unnatural abilities and often withdrew from society.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, keluarga osaki mochi secara historis dijauhi dan dicurigai karena kemampuan tak wajar mereka, dan sering menarik diri dari masyarakat.
claims.quote: Osaki mochi families were historically shunned and mistrusted for their unnatural abilities. They often withdrew from society and avoided contact with the outside world.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, osaki live in the mountains but also find their way into human villages and homes.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, osaki hidup di pegunungan tetapi juga masuk ke desa dan rumah manusia.
claims.quote: Osaki live in the mountains, but also find their ways into human villages and homes.

claims.statement: Qiuniu is one of the nine dragon sons in an account by Li Dongyang.
claims.statement_id: Qiuniu adalah salah satu dari sembilan putra naga dalam kisah Li Dongyang.
claims.quote: 囚牛（しゅうぎゅう）は、李東陽が著した『懐麓堂集』の説による竜生九子の一つ。姿は黄色い小さな龍の角と鱗を持つ。

claims.statement: Its image includes a small yellow dragon’s horns and scales.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya memiliki tanduk dan sisik naga kuning kecil.
claims.quote: 囚牛（しゅうぎゅう）は、李東陽が著した『懐麓堂集』の説による竜生九子の一つ。姿は黄色い小さな龍の角と鱗を持つ。

claims.statement: It is associated with music and decorates string and percussion instruments.
claims.statement_id: Ia dikaitkan dengan musik dan menghiasi alat musik petik serta perkusi.
claims.quote: 音楽を好み、琴や鼓の飾りになっている。イー族の月琴、ペー族（白族：雲南省）の琴、他チベット系民族のいくつか楽器で見られる。

claims.statement: Examples occur on instruments of Yi, Bai and Tibetan-related peoples.
claims.statement_id: Contohnya terdapat pada alat musik masyarakat Yi, Bai, dan kelompok terkait Tibet.
claims.quote: 音楽を好み、琴や鼓の飾りになっている。イー族の月琴、ペー族（白族：雲南省）の琴、他チベット系民族のいくつか楽器で見られる。

claims.statement: Chinese Wikipedia calls Qiuniu the eldest of the Nine Sons of the Dragon and quotes Li Dongyang of the Ming Dynasty in the Huailutang ji, section "Ji longsheng jiuzi": "Qiuniu, a dragon kind, loved music all his life; the beast carved on the head of the huqin today is his remaining image."
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Mandarin menyebut Qiuniu putra sulung dari Sembilan Putra Naga; ia mengutip Li Dongyang (Dinasti Ming) dalam Huailutang ji, bagian "Ji longsheng jiuzi": "Qiuniu, jenis naga, seumur hidup gemar musik; binatang yang kini diukir di kepala huqin adalah wujud peninggalannya."
claims.quote: 囚牛，龍生九子中的長子，明朝李東陽所著《懷麓堂集》之〈記龍生九子〉篇中所記：「囚牛，龍種，平生好音樂，今胡琴頭上刻獸是其遺像。」

claims.statement: According to Chinese Wikipedia, its shape is a small yellow dragon with scales and horns; it loved music and playing the qin and was highly skilled in music, so many qin heads use its likeness.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Mandarin, bentuknya naga kecil kuning bersisik dan bertanduk; ia sangat menyukai musik dan gemar memainkan qin dengan keahlian tinggi, sehingga banyak kepala qin memakai wujudnya.
claims.quote: 形狀為有鱗角的黃色小龍，平生很喜歡音樂，酷愛彈琴，對音樂有很高的造詣，所以很多琴頭都用祂的造像。

claims.statement: According to Chinese Wikipedia, its raised-head, open-mouthed image is also found on the Han huqin, the Yi dragon-head yueqin, the Bai sanxian and some Tibetan instruments.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Mandarin, wujudnya dengan kepala terangkat dan mulut terbuka juga terdapat pada huqin suku Han, yueqin berkepala naga suku Yi, sanxian suku Bai, dan sebagian alat musik suku Tibet.
claims.quote: 例如：漢族的胡琴、彝族的龍頭月琴、白族的三弦琴以及藏族的一些樂器上也有其揚頭張口的形象。

claims.statement: English Wikipedia names Li Dongyang's (1447–1516) list, with 9 creatures, as one of four principal versions of the list of the dragon's children.
claims.statement_id: Wikipedia bahasa Inggris menyebut daftar Li Dongyang (1447–1516), yang memuat 9 makhluk, sebagai salah satu dari empat versi utama daftar putra naga.
claims.quote: There are four principal versions of the list: ... Li Dongyang's (李東陽 , 1447–1516) list, which includes 9 creatures

claims.statement: Several Ming Dynasty texts list what were claimed as the Nine Offspring of the Dragon, and subsequently these feature prominently in popular Chinese stories and writings.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa teks Dinasti Ming memuat apa yang diklaim sebagai Sembilan Putra Naga, dan sejak itu menonjol dalam kisah dan tulisan populer Tiongkok.
claims.quote: Several Ming Dynasty texts list what were claimed as the Nine Offspring of the Dragon (Chinese: 龍生九子), and subsequently these feature prominently in popular Chinese stories and writings.

claims.statement: According to English Wikipedia, some of these creatures are based on earlier mythological beasts such as pulao or bixi, but most have no other mythological background and are merely used as names for decorative structures.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Wikipedia bahasa Inggris, sebagian makhluk dalam daftar itu berdasar pada makhluk mitologis yang lebih tua seperti pulao atau bixi, tetapi kebanyakan tidak punya latar mitologis lain dan hanya dipakai sebagai nama struktur dekoratif.
claims.quote: Some of these creatures are based on earlier mythological beasts, such as pulao or bixi, but most of them have no other mythological background and are merely used as names for decorative structures.

claims.statement: Rōjinbi is a supernatural fire in Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.
claims.statement_id: Rōjinbi adalah api gaib dalam Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.
claims.quote: The Rōjinbi (老人火 ; literally, 'old person fire') or rōjin no hi (老人の火 ) (same meaning) is a kind of supernatural fire that appears in the Edo period bestiary Ehon Hyaku Monogatari.

claims.statement: Its stories place it in mountains on rainy nights.
claims.statement_id: Ceritanya menempatkannya di pegunungan pada malam hujan.
claims.quote: The rōjinbi is a demonic flame that supposedly appears deep in the mountains on rainy nights on the boundary of Shinano Province (now Nagano Prefecture) and Tōtōmi Province (now Shizuoka Prefecture).

claims.statement: It appears with an elderly person.
claims.statement_id: Ia muncul bersama orang tua.
claims.quote: It is said to appear along with an elderly person, and cannot be extinguished by water but can be if beat with animal skins.

claims.statement: A tale says water cannot extinguish it but animal skins can.
claims.statement_id: Satu cerita menyebut air tidak dapat memadamkannya, tetapi kulit hewan dapat.
claims.quote: It is said to appear along with an elderly person, and cannot be extinguished by water but can be if beat with animal skins.

claims.statement: Holding footwear overhead is said to divert it onto another path.
claims.statement_id: Mengangkat alas kaki di atas kepala konon mengalihkannya ke jalur lain.
claims.quote: If, for instance, one comes across a rōjinbi on a straight stretch of road, holding one's footwear over one's head will prompt it to veer off to another path.

claims.statement: It pursues a person who panics and runs away.
claims.statement_id: Ia mengejar orang yang panik lalu melarikan diri.
claims.quote: However, if the person panics and tries to run away, it will apparently pursue them indefinitely.

claims.statement: According to the Digital Daijisen Plus, the rōjinbi is a strange phenomenon from Japan: an eerie fire that appears with an old man deep in the mountains on rainy nights, is not put out by pouring water, chases those who flee in fright, but can be got past by placing footwear on one's head; traditions remain in Nagano and Shizuoka Prefectures.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Digital Daijisen Plus, rōjinbi adalah gejala aneh dari Jepang: api aneh yang muncul bersama seorang tua di pegunungan dalam pada malam hujan, tidak padam disiram air, mengejar orang yang kabur ketakutan, tetapi dapat dilewati bila seseorang meletakkan alas kaki di kepala; tradisinya ada di Prefektur Nagano dan Shizuoka.
claims.quote: 老人火(ろうじんび) 日本に伝わる怪現象。雨の夜の山奥に老人とともに現れる怪火。水をかけても消えず、驚いて逃げると追いかけてくるが、頭に履物を載せればやり過ごすことができるとされる。長野県・静岡県に伝承が残る。

claims.statement: It is sometimes called "tengu no miakashi" (天狗の御燈, "tengu's lantern"), but this actually means an onibi that a tengu has lit.
claims.statement_id: Kadang disebut "tengu no miakashi" (天狗の御燈, "lentera tengu"), tetapi sebenarnya itu berarti onibi yang dinyalakan tengu.
claims.quote: It is sometimes called 'tengu no miakashi' (天狗の御燈 ; literally, 'tengu's lantern'), but this actually means an onibi that a tengu has lit.

claims.statement: The tengu trait of hating beasts and meat, as described in Senkyō ibun and Heisuiroku, has been pointed out as related to the rumor that rōjinbi can be put out with animal skins.
claims.statement_id: Sifat tengu yang membenci binatang dan daging, sebagaimana dalam Senkyō ibun dan Heisuiroku, dikaitkan dengan kabar bahwa rōjinbi dapat dipadamkan dengan kulit binatang.
claims.quote: The priest was assumed to be a tengu, and the tengu trait of hating beasts and meat as described in Senkyō ibun and Heisuiroku has been pointed out as being related to the rumour that rōjinbi can be put out with animal skins.

claims.statement: Shichinin misaki are a group of ghosts in Shikoku and Chūgoku traditions.
claims.statement_id: Shichinin misaki adalah kelompok hantu dalam tradisi Shikoku dan Chūgoku.
claims.quote: The Shichinin misaki (七人ミサキ or 七人みさき), which means "7-person misaki," are a group of ghosts first known in Kōchi Prefecture, told about in the Shikoku and Chūgoku regions.

claims.statement: They are associated with people killed in disasters and drowning.
claims.statement_id: Mereka dikaitkan dengan orang yang meninggal akibat bencana dan tenggelam.
claims.quote: They are ghosts of humans who died from calamities and accidents, especially drowning at sea.

claims.statement: The group has seven members and appears near water.
claims.statement_id: Kelompok itu beranggota tujuh dan muncul dekat air.
claims.quote: As according to its name, they normally, together as a group of seven, appear mainly near water, like seas and rivers.

claims.statement: An encounter is said to cause fatal fever.
claims.statement_id: Pertemuan dengan mereka konon menyebabkan demam yang mematikan.
