claims.quote: Humans who encounter the shichinin misaki experience a high fever, and die.

claims.statement: A victim replaces a spirit that gains release.
claims.statement_id: Korban menggantikan roh yang memperoleh kebebasan.
claims.quote: By possessing and killing one person, one of the spirits of the shichinin misaki are able to go to peace, and in its place, the one who was possessed and killed becomes one of the shichinin misaki.

claims.statement: The group therefore remains at seven members.
claims.statement_id: Karena itu kelompok tersebut tetap beranggota tujuh.
claims.quote: For this reason, the shichinin misaki are always a group of seven, never increasing nor decreasing.

claims.statement: Yokai.com writes the name as 七人ミサキ, translates it "the seven spirits", gives the habitat as usually near bodies of water, and says it survives solely on vengeance.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis namanya 七人ミサキ, menerjemahkannya "tujuh roh", dan menyebut habitatnya biasanya dekat perairan; ia bertahan hidup semata-mata dari dendam.
claims.quote: Shichinin misaki 七人ミサキ しちにんみさき Translation: the seven spirits Habitat: usually encountered near bodies of water Diet: none; survives solely on vengeance

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the shichinin misaki are a band of seven ghosts in Shikoku and Western Japan, most often met near water such as the seashore or riverbanks, always seven in number, and they bring disaster upon any who meet them.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, shichinin misaki adalah kelompok tujuh hantu di Shikoku dan Jepang Barat, paling sering ditemui di dekat perairan seperti pantai atau tepi sungai, selalu berjumlah tujuh, dan mendatangkan bencana bagi siapa pun yang bertemu mereka.
claims.quote: The shichinin misaki are a band of seven ghosts who appear in Shikoku and Western Japan. They are most often encountered near bodies of water, such as along the seashore or by riverbanks. They are always seven in number, and the bring disaster upon any who meet them.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, people who encounter the shichinin misaki almost always die shortly after, frequently from a mysterious and deadly fever.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, orang yang bertemu shichinin misaki hampir selalu mati tak lama kemudian, sering berupa demam misterius yang mematikan.
claims.quote: People who encounter the shichinin misaki almost always die shortly after. Frequently this take the form of a mysterious and deadly fever.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the word misaki (御先) means "one who goes before" and has a number of nuanced meanings.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, kata misaki (御先) berarti "yang berjalan di depan" dan punya beberapa nuansa makna.
claims.quote: The word misaki (御先) means “one who goes before,” and has a number of nuanced meanings.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, some theories describe them as spirits of Taira soldiers who died in a boar trap during the Genpei War, of seven wicked priests murdered by townspeople, or of seven women pilgrims thrown overboard and drowned.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ada teori yang menyebut mereka roh prajurit Taira yang tewas di perangkap babi hutan saat Perang Genpei, tujuh pendeta jahat yang dibunuh warga kota, atau tujuh peziarah perempuan yang dilempar ke laut dan tenggelam.
claims.quote: Some theories describe them as the spirits of Taira soldiers who died in a boar trap while fleeing their enemies during the Genpei War. Others attribute them to the spirits of seven wicked priests who were murdered by a group of townspeople they were tormenting. Others say they are the spirits of seven women pilgrims who were thrown overboard at sea and drowned.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Chikazane's seven retainers also followed him into death by suicide; afterward strange occurrences around their graves were attributed to their restless, vengeful spirits.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, tujuh pengikut Chikazane juga mati bunuh diri menyusulnya; sesudah itu terjadi keanehan di makam mereka yang dikaitkan dengan roh mereka yang gelisah dan pendendam.
claims.quote: Chikazane’s seven retainers also followed him into death by suicide. After that, strange occurrences were reported around the graves of Chikazane and his retainers. These were attributed to their restless, vengeful spirits.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, Motochika held services to appease the spirits of Chikazane and his retainers and built a shrine in Chikazane's name (the Kira Shrine in Kōchi City), but none of this stopped the vengeance of the shichinin misaki.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, Motochika mengadakan ritual untuk menenangkan roh Chikazane dan para pengikutnya dan membangun kuil atas nama Chikazane (Kuil Kira di Kota Kōchi), tetapi semua itu tidak menghentikan dendam shichinin misaki.
claims.quote: Hearing the story of the shichinin misaki, Motochika performed services to appease the restless spirits of Chikazane and his retainers. He built a shrine in Chikazane’s name, which still stands today (the Kira Shrine in Kōchi City); however, none of these had any effect at stopping the vengeance of the shichinin misaki.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, even today the shichinin misaki are said to haunt Western Japan and Shikoku, Kōchi City in particular, and traffic accidents and other strange occurrences are blamed on their spirits.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, hingga kini shichinin misaki dikatakan menghantui Jepang Barat dan Shikoku, terutama Kota Kōchi, dan kecelakaan lalu lintas serta keanehan lain disalahkan pada roh mereka.
claims.quote: Even today, the shichinin misaki are said to haunt Western Japan and Shikoku, and Kōchi City in particular. Traffic accidents and other strange occurrences are blamed on the restless spirits of the shichinin misaki.

claims.statement: In Mihara, Hiroshima Prefecture, there was a mound called "Kyouzuka" where seven brutal mountain priests were killed by the people they tormented; their vengeful spirits became the shichinin misaki, and the mound is said to have been made to pacify that curse.
claims.statement_id: Di Mihara, Prefektur Hiroshima, ada gundukan "Kyouzuka" tempat tujuh pendeta gunung kejam dibunuh orang-orang yang mereka siksa; roh pendendam mereka menjadi shichinin misaki, dan gundukan itu dikatakan dibuat untuk menenangkan kutukan itu.
claims.quote: In Mihara, Hiroshima Prefecture, there was a mound called "Kyouzuka" (経塚, "sutra mound" or 狂塚, "insanity mound"), where there were once 7 brutal mountain priests, and when the people they tormented worked together to kill them, their vengeful spirits became the shichinin misaki, and it is said that this mound was made in order to pacify that curse.

claims.statement: In Touyama, Yamaguchi Prefecture, shichinin misaki are said to appear as monks, ringing bells, walking paths at high speed and kidnapping female children.
claims.statement_id: Di Touyama, Prefektur Yamaguchi, shichinin misaki dikatakan tampil sebagai biksu sambil membunyikan lonceng, berjalan cepat di jalan, dan menculik anak perempuan.
claims.quote: In Touyama, Yamaguchi Prefecture (now Shūnan), it is said that shichinin misai appearing as monks, while ringing bells, would walk down paths at high speed, and kidnap female children.

claims.statement: Girls were warned not to go outside after dark; when it was necessary, it is said one can flee from the shichinin misaki by going about hiding one's thumb in one's hand.
claims.statement_id: Anak perempuan diperingatkan tidak keluar setelah gelap; bila terpaksa, dikatakan orang dapat lolos dari shichinin misaki dengan berjalan sambil menyembunyikan ibu jari di dalam genggaman.
claims.quote: For that reason, girls were warned not go outside after it has gotten dark, but in times when it was necessary to go outside, it is said that it is possible to flee from the shichinin misaki by going about while hiding one's thumb in one's hand.

claims.statement: Shidaidaka is a yōkai of the Chūgoku region.
claims.statement_id: Shidaidaka adalah yōkai dari wilayah Chūgoku.
claims.quote: Shidaidaka (次第高) are a yōkai of the Chūgoku region.

claims.statement: Its humanoid form grows taller when observers look up.
claims.statement_id: Wujudnya menyerupai manusia dan bertambah tinggi ketika orang mendongak.
claims.quote: It is a humanoid yōkai that appears above roads, and when those that see it look up, the shidaidaka would accordingly grow taller.

claims.statement: It becomes shorter when the observer looks down.
claims.statement_id: Ia menjadi lebih pendek ketika orang menunduk.
claims.quote: In reverse, if one looks down it becomes shorter, but if one doesn't look down, it would steadily grow taller.

claims.statement: Continued downward looking is said to make it disappear.
claims.statement_id: Terus melihat ke bawah konon membuatnya menghilang.
claims.quote: In reverse, if one looks further and further downwards, the shidaidaka would steadily become smaller, and then disappear.

claims.statement: One local account forbids looking at it from between the thighs.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah setempat melarang melihatnya dari antara paha.
claims.quote: In Sakurae, Ōchi District, Shimane Prefecture (now Gōtsu), in a place called Kawato, when a shidaidaka appears, one must never look at it from beneath one's thighs.

claims.statement: It is regarded as a type of mikoshi-nyūdō.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap sebagai jenis mikoshi-nyūdō.
claims.quote: It is a type of mikoshi-nyūdō, and is thus of the same type as the taka-nyūdō

claims.statement: According to the Digital Daijisen Plus, the shidaidaka is a yōkai of the Chūgoku and Shikoku regions that grows so tall that one looks up and shrinks when one looks down; it is also called "taka nyūdō", and similar to the mikoshi nyūdō, miage nyūdō and nyūdō-bōzu.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Digital Daijisen Plus, shidaidaka adalah yōkai dari wilayah Chūgoku dan Shikoku yang menjadi tinggi sampai orang menengadah dan mengecil bila orang menunduk; disebut juga "taka nyūdō", dan serupa dengan mikoshi nyūdō, miage nyūdō, dan nyūdō-bōzu.
claims.quote: 次第高(しだいだか) 日本の妖怪。中国・四国地方に伝わるもので、見上げるほど背が高くなり、見下ろせば小さくなる。「高入道」とも。類似のものに「見越入道」「見上げ入道」「入道坊主」などがある。

claims.statement: Therefore, if one meets a shidaidaka, one must never look up.
claims.statement_id: Karena itu, bila bertemu shidaidaka, orang tidak boleh menengadah.
claims.quote: Therefore, if one ever meets a Shidaidaka, then one must never look up.

claims.statement: According to a folktale in Hazumi, Ōchi, Shimane Prefecture, when hunting it is best to leave at least one last bullet to kill a shidaidaka should it appear.
claims.statement_id: Menurut kisah rakyat Hazumi, Ōchi, Prefektur Shimane, saat berburu sebaiknya menyisakan setidaknya satu peluru terakhir untuk membunuh shidaidaka bila ia muncul.
claims.quote: According to a folktale in Hazumi, Ōchi, Shimane Prefecture, it is said that when one goes out on a hunt, whatever spoils one gets, it is best to leave at least one last bullet to prepare for when a shidaidaka would appear in order to kill it.

claims.statement: In Matsukawa, Gōtsu, the shidaidaka is said to be the boss of nekomata, and when a hunter brought one down, its true form was indeed a nekomata.
claims.statement_id: Di Matsukawa, Gōtsu, shidaidaka dikatakan pemimpin nekomata, dan ketika seorang pemburu menjatuhkan shidaidaka, wujud aslinya memang nekomata.
claims.quote: In Matsukawa, Gōtsu, Shidaidaka are also said to be the boss of nekomata, and when a certain hunter went to bring down a shidaidaka, its true form was, as thought, a nekomata.

claims.statement: Yokai.com, in its taka nyūdō entry (another name of the shidaidaka according to Kotobank), says it is usually encountered in alleyways, suddenly appearing before humans; like the mikoshi nyūdō, it increases its height at the same speed as its victim's gaze.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com, pada entri taka nyūdō (nama lain shidaidaka menurut Kotobank), menyebut makhluk ini biasanya ditemui di gang dan tiba-tiba muncul di depan orang; seperti mikoshi nyūdō, tingginya bertambah secepat pandangan korban.
claims.quote: Taka nyūdō are usually encountered in alleyways, suddenly appearing before unsuspecting humans. Like the mikoshi nyūdō, they increase their height at the same speed as their victim’s gaze.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com (taka nyūdō entry), it can be defeated like the mikoshi nyūdō: by showing courage and no fear and refusing to raise one's head, denying it the chance to grow.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com (entri taka nyūdō), makhluk ini dapat dikalahkan seperti mikoshi nyūdō: menunjukkan keberanian, tidak takut, dan menolak mengangkat kepala sehingga ia tidak sempat tumbuh.
claims.quote: Taka nyūdō can be defeated in a similar manner as the mikoshi nyūdō—by demonstrating courage in the face of death, showing no fear, and refusing to raise your head and denying them the chance to grow.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com (taka nyūdō entry), some say it can be outsmarted by carrying a ruler or other measuring utensil and calculating its height before it can react.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com (entri taka nyūdō), sebagian orang berkata makhluk ini dapat dikelabui dengan membawa penggaris atau alat ukur dan menghitung tingginya sebelum ia bereaksi.
claims.quote: Some say they can also be outsmarted by carrying a ruler or other measuring utensils and attempting to calculate their height before it can react.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com (taka nyūdō entry), it is generally less violent than other giants, content with scaring its victims rather than ripping their throats out or crushing them with trees.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com (entri taka nyūdō), makhluk ini umumnya kurang ganas dibanding raksasa lain; ia cukup menakut-nakuti korbannya, bukan merobek leher atau meremukkan mereka dengan pohon.
claims.quote: Taka nyūdō are generally less violent than other giants. They are content with simply scaring its victims instead of ripping their throats out or crushing them with trees.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com (taka nyūdō entry), its true form is often a tanuki, kitsune or kawauso.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com (entri taka nyūdō), wujud aslinya sering berupa tanuki, kitsune, atau kawauso.
claims.quote: Its true form is often a tanuki, kitsune, or kawauso.

claims.statement: Shippeitarō is a helper dog in a Japanese folktale.
claims.statement_id: Shippeitarō adalah anjing penolong dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Shippeitaro or Shippei Taro (German spelling: Schippeitaro; Japanese: しっぺい太郎 or 竹篦太郎 ) is the name of a helper dog in the Japanese fairy tale by the same name.

claims.statement: A warrior learns that spirits fear this dog.
claims.statement_id: Seorang pendekar mengetahui bahwa para roh takut pada anjing ini.
claims.quote: A young warrior overhears the spirits hinting that their would-be bane was "Shippeitaro", which turns out to be a dog.

claims.statement: The warrior and dog defeat spirits after the dog replaces a sacrificial maiden.
claims.statement_id: Pendekar dan anjing mengalahkan para roh setelah anjing menggantikan perempuan yang akan dikorbankan.
claims.quote: This dog is substituted for the maiden to be placed inside the sacrificial container, and when the spirits arrive, the warrior and dog attack the cats and vanquish them.

claims.statement: Many versions portray the hostile spirits as monkeys.
claims.statement_id: Banyak versi menggambarkan para roh bermusuhan sebagai monyet.
claims.quote: The evil spirits appear as monkeys in most instances of the tale, as in the version of "Shippei Taro" given in Keigo Seki's anthology (translated into English 1963).

claims.statement: Folklorists classify it as the Destroying the Monkey Demon tale type.
claims.statement_id: Peneliti cerita rakyat menggolongkannya sebagai tipe cerita Mengalahkan Setan Monyet.
claims.quote: "Destroying the Monkey Demon" (Sarugami taiji) tale type by Japanese folklorists.

claims.statement: One translated version instead gives the spirits feline forms.
claims.statement_id: Satu versi terjemahan justru memberi para roh wujud kucing.
claims.quote: James's "Schippeitaro" (1888), which share the same plotline: The mountain spirit and its minions (in the guise of cats in this version) demand a yearly human sacrifice of a maiden from the local village.

claims.statement: In the Violet Fairy Book version, in the forest chapel the youth sees a troop of hideous cats dancing furiously and hears them cry that Schippeitaro must not be told and it must be kept hidden.
claims.statement_id: Dalam versi The Violet Fairy Book, di kapel hutan sang pemuda melihat sekawanan kucing buruk rupa menari beringas dan mendengar mereka berseru agar jangan memberi tahu Schippeitaro dan merahasiakannya.
claims.quote: he saw a troop of hideous cats, dancing furiously, making the night horrible with their yells. ... he could make out the words, ‘Do not tell Schippeitaro! Keep it hidden and secret! Do not tell Schippeitaro!’

claims.statement: The villagers answer that Schippeitaro is the great dog belonging to their prince's overseer.
claims.statement_id: Penduduk menjawab bahwa Schippeitaro adalah anjing besar milik pengawas pangeran mereka.
claims.quote: ‘Schippeitaro is the great dog that belongs to the overseer of our prince,’

claims.statement: The village's sorrow is caused by the Spirit of the Mountain, to whom a maiden must be furnished every year to eat.
claims.statement_id: Kesedihan desa disebabkan Roh Gunung, yang setiap tahun harus diberi seorang gadis untuk dimakan.
claims.quote: all this sorrow was caused by the Spirit of the Mountain, to whom every year they were bound to furnish a maiden for him to eat.

claims.statement: At the next midnight the cats bring a huge black cat who seems to be their king and whom the young man guesses to be the Spirit of the Mountain.
claims.statement_id: Pada tengah malam berikutnya para kucing membawa seekor kucing hitam raksasa yang tampak seperti raja mereka dan diduga sang pemuda sebagai Roh Gunung.
claims.quote: But this time they had in their midst a huge black cat who seemed to be their king, and whom the young man guessed to be the Spirit of the Mountain.

claims.statement: Instead of biting a maiden's neck, Schippeitaro's teeth fastened in the monster cat, and the youth cut off its head with his sword.
claims.statement_id: Alih-alih menggigit leher seorang gadis, gigi Schippeitaro menancap pada kucing raksasa itu, dan sang pemuda memenggal kepalanya dengan pedang.
claims.quote: But instead of fastening his teeth in the neck of a beautiful maiden, Schippeitaro’s teeth were fastened in HIM, and the youth ran up and cut off his head with his sword.

claims.statement: At sunrise the brave dog was returned to his master; from then on the mountain girls were safe and every year a feast was held in memory of the young warrior and the dog Schippeitaro.
claims.statement_id: Saat matahari terbit anjing pemberani itu dikembalikan kepada tuannya; sejak itu gadis-gadis gunung aman dan setiap tahun diadakan pesta untuk mengenang sang pemuda dan anjing Schippeitaro.
claims.quote: At sunrise the brave dog was taken back to his master, and from that time the mountain girls were safe, and every year a feast was held in memory of the young warrior and the dog Schippeitaro.

claims.statement: Takiribime (also Takirihime or Tagirihime) is a goddess in Japanese mythology, one of the three Munakata goddesses.
claims.statement_id: Takiribime (juga Takirihime atau Tagirihime) adalah dewi dalam mitologi Jepang, salah satu dari tiga dewi Munakata.
claims.quote: タキリビメ（タキリヒメまたはタギリヒメとも）は、日本神話に登場する女神。宗像三女神の一柱で宗像大社では「田心姫神」として、沖ノ島にある沖津宮に祀られている。

claims.statement: She is worshipped at the Okitsu shrine on Okinoshima.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja di Kuil Okitsu di Okinoshima.
claims.quote: タキリビメ（タキリヒメまたはタギリヒメとも）は、日本神話に登場する女神。宗像三女神の一柱で宗像大社では「田心姫神」として、沖ノ島にある沖津宮に祀られている。

claims.statement: She was born from the oath of Amaterasu and Susanoo as one of the three Munakata goddesses; the Kojiki writes her name Takiribime, the Nihon Shoki Tagorihime or Takirihime.
claims.statement_id: Ia lahir dari ukei Amaterasu dan Susanoo sebagai salah satu dari tiga dewi Munakata; Kojiki menulis namanya Takiribime, Nihon Shoki menulis Tagorihime atau Takirihime.
claims.quote: 天照大御神と須佐之男命の誓約により誕生した「宗像三女神」の一柱で、『古事記』では多紀理毘売命、『日本書紀』では田心姫（たごりひめ）・田霧姫（たきりひめ）と表記される。

claims.statement: The Kojiki names two children with Ōkuninushi.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menyebut dua anaknya bersama Ōkuninushi.
claims.quote: 『古事記』の大国主の系譜では、大国主神との間に阿遅鉏高日子根神（あぢすきたかひこね・味耜高彦根神）と下照比売（したてるひめ）を生んだと記されている。

claims.statement: According to the Kokugakuin University Kojiki database synopsis, in the ukei between Amaterasu and Susanoo, three goddesses were born by Amaterasu from Susanoo's ten-fist sword and became Susanoo's children; Takiribime is the first, also called Okitsushimahime, enshrined at the Okitsu-miya of Munakata, and the three are the "three great deities" worshipped by the Munakata clan.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ringkasan basis data Kojiki Universitas Kokugakuin, dalam ukei antara Amaterasu dan Susanoo, tiga dewi lahir dari pedang jūken Susanoo oleh Amaterasu dan menjadi anak Susanoo; Takiribime yang pertama, juga disebut Okitsushimahime, bersemayam di Okitsu-miya di Munakata, dan ketiganya adalah "tiga dewa agung" yang dipuja klan Munakata.
claims.quote: 天照大御神と須佐之男命とのうけい（誓約）において、天照大御神によって須佐之男命の身につけていた十拳剣から生まれ、須佐之男命の子となった三女神（多紀理毘売命・市寸島比売命・多岐都比売命）の第一。別名を奥津島比売命といい、胸形の奥津宮に鎮座する。この三柱の神は胸形君らがもちいつく（奉斎する）三前の大神であるという。

claims.statement: With Ōkuninushi she bore Ajisukitakahikone (Kamo no Ōmikami) and Takahime (Shitateruhime).
claims.statement_id: Dengan Ōkuninushi ia melahirkan Ajisukitakahikone (Kamo no Ōmikami) dan Takahime (Shitateruhime).
claims.quote: また、大国主神との間に阿遅鉏高日子根神（迦毛大御神）と高比売命（下光比売命）を生んでいる。

claims.statement: One view reads the name Takiribime with "ta" as a prefix and "kiri" as mist, a deity associated with mist.
claims.statement_id: Satu tafsir memahami nama Takiribime dengan "ta" sebagai awalan dan "kiri" sebagai kabut, yaitu dewi yang berkaitan dengan kabut.
claims.quote: 多紀理毘売命の名義は、タを接頭辞、キリを霧と解し、霧にまつわる神とする説がある。

claims.statement: The Munakata shrine consists of three shrines enshrining the three goddesses respectively at the Okitsu-miya (Okinoshima), Nakatsu-miya (Ōshima) and Hetsu-miya (Tashima, inland).
claims.statement_id: Kuil Munakata terdiri dari tiga kuil yang memuja ketiga dewi masing-masing di Okitsu-miya (Okinoshima), Nakatsu-miya (Ōshima), dan Hetsu-miya (Tashima, di daratan).
claims.quote: 宗像神社は三宮からなり、三女神をそれぞれ沖津宮（沖ノ島）・中津宮（大島）・辺津宮（田島。内陸に所在）に祭っている。

claims.statement: According to the tradition of Munakata Taisha, the Okitsu-miya enshrines Tagorihime, the Nakatsu-miya Tagitsuhime and the Hetsu-miya Ichikishimahime, and they are worshipped so to this day.
claims.statement_id: Menurut tradisi Munakata Taisha, Okitsu-miya memuja Tagori-hime (Tagoribime), Nakatsu-miya memuja Tagitsuhime, dan Hetsu-miya memuja Ichikishimahime, dan hingga kini dipuja demikian.
claims.quote: 宗像大社の社伝では、紀の本書と同様、沖津宮が田心姫神、中津宮が湍津姫神、辺津宮が市杵島姫神となっており、現在までそれに則って祭られている。

claims.statement: Okinoshima in the Genkai Sea is the center of the Munakata shrine's rites, whose worship seems to have been treated as nationally important early on for diplomacy, especially exchange with the Korean Peninsula.
claims.statement_id: Okinoshima di Laut Genkai adalah pusat upacara kuil Munakata, dan upacaranya sejak lama dipandang penting oleh negara dalam diplomasi dan pertukaran dengan Semenanjung Korea.
claims.quote: 玄界灘に浮かぶ沖ノ島は、宗像神社の祭りの中心であり、外交、特に朝鮮半島との交流に当たって、古くその祭祀が国家的に重視されていたと見られる。

claims.statement: Behind the Okitsu-miya shrine building on Okinoshima, 23 ritual sites have been found confirming rites continued from the latter half of the fourth century to the ninth century.
claims.statement_id: Di belakang bangunan Okitsu-miya di Okinoshima ditemukan 23 situs ritual yang menunjukkan upacara berlangsung terus dari paruh akhir abad ke-4 hingga abad ke-9.
claims.quote: 沖ノ島の沖津宮社殿の背後には、山頂から転落してできた巨岩群があり、その岩上や岩裾に23箇所の祭祀遺跡が見つかっていて、四世紀後半から九世紀にかけて祭祀が継続して行われていたことが確かめられる。

claims.statement: Tamakushi-hime is a goddess in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Tamakushi-hime adalah dewi dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Tamakushi-hime (玉櫛媛, タマクシヒメ) also known as Mishimanomizokui-hime (三嶋溝熾姫, ミシマノミゾクイヒメ) and Seyadatarahime (セヤダタラヒメ), is a feminine deity who appears in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: Mishimanomizokui-hime is one of her alternate names.
claims.statement_id: Mishimanomizokui-hime adalah salah satu nama lainnya.
claims.quote: Tamakushi-hime (玉櫛媛, タマクシヒメ) also known as Mishimanomizokui-hime (三嶋溝熾姫, ミシマノミゾクイヒメ) and Seyadatarahime (セヤダタラヒメ), is a feminine deity who appears in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: She is named as the mother of Himetataraisuzu-hime.
claims.statement_id: Ia disebut sebagai ibu Himetataraisuzu-hime.
claims.quote: She is known as the mother of Himetataraisuzu-hime, the first empress of Japan, Kamo no Okimi, a distant ancestor of the Miwa clan, Kamigamo the deity of Kamigamo Shrine.

claims.statement: Several additional princess names are associated with her.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa nama putri lainnya dikaitkan dengannya.
claims.quote: She is also known as Princess Mishima-Mizo, Seiyadatarahihime, Katsutamayori-biyorihime and Kimikahihime.

claims.statement: According to the Digital Nihonjinmei Daijiten Plus, Tamakushihime is a woman who appears in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, daughter of Mishima no Mizokuimimi no Kami, who married Kotoshironushi and bore Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime no Mikoto; in the Kojiki she is called Seyadatarahime.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Digital Nihonjinmei Daijiten Plus, Tamakushihime adalah perempuan yang muncul dalam Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki, putri Mishima no Mizokuimimi no Kami, menikah dengan Kotoshironushi dan melahirkan Hime-tatara-isuzu-hime no Mikoto; dalam Kojiki ia disebut Seyadatarahime.
claims.quote: 玉櫛媛 たまくしひめ 記・紀にみえる女性。 三島溝橛耳神(みしまのみぞくいみみのかみ)の娘。事代主神(ことしろぬしのかみ)と結婚。媛蹈鞴五十鈴媛命(ひめたたらいすずひめのみこと)を生んだ。「古事記」では勢夜陀多良比売(せやだたらひめ)という。

claims.statement: In Aston's translation of the Nihongi, Hime-tatara-i-suzu-hime was born to Koto-shiro-nushi no Kami and Tama-kushi-hime, daughter of Mizo-kuhi-ni no Kami of Mishima.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston atas Nihongi, Hime-tatara-i-suzu-hime lahir dari Koto-shiro-nushi no Kami dan Tama-kushi-hime, putri Mizo-kuhi-ni no Kami dari Mishima.
claims.quote: born to Koto-shiro-nushi no Kami by his union with Tama-kushi-hime, daughter of Mizo-kuhi-ni no Kami of Mishima. Her name is Hime-tatara-i-suzu-hime no Mikoto.

claims.statement: In the Nihongi, the Emperor was rejoiced and on the 24th day of the 9th month received Hime-tatara-i-suzu-hime no Mikoto as his wife.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Nihongi, kaisar bergembira dan pada hari ke-24 bulan ke-9 menerima Hime-tatara-i-suzu-hime no Mikoto sebagai istrinya.
claims.quote: The Emperor was rejoiced, and on the 24th day of the 9th month he received Hime-tatara-i-suzu-hime no Mikoto and made her his wife.

claims.statement: The English Wikipedia infobox lists spouse Kotoshironushi (Nihon Shoki) or Ōmononushi (Kojiki), issue Kamo no Okimi, Himetataraisuzu-hime, Isuzuyori-hime and Kamowakeikazuchi-no-mikoto, and father Kamotaketsunumi no Mikoto.
claims.statement_id: Kotak info Wikipedia bahasa Inggris mencantumkan suami Kotoshironushi (Nihon Shoki) atau Ōmononushi (Kojiki), anak Kamo no Okimi, Himetataraisuzu-hime, Isuzuyori-hime, dan Kamowakeikazuchi-no-mikoto, serta ayah Kamotaketsunumi no Mikoto.
claims.quote: Spouse Kotoshironushi (Nihon Shoki), or Ōmononushi (Kojiki) Issue Kamo no Okimi, Himetataraisuzu-hime, Isuzuyori-hime, Kamowakeikazuchi-no-mikoto [ja] Father Kamotaketsunumi no Mikoto

claims.statement: Tamanooya is a kami in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Tamanooya adalah kami dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Tamanooya-no-Mikoto (玉祖命), also known as Tamanoya, is a kami from Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: He is credited with creating the imperial jewel.
claims.statement_id: Ia dianggap sebagai pembuat permata kekaisaran.
claims.quote: Tamanooya is believed to be the creator of Yasakani no Magatama, one of the three imperial regalia of Japan - commonly referred to as the “Jewel” (along with the sword and the mirror).

claims.statement: He helps the plan to bring Amaterasu out of her cave.
claims.statement_id: Ia membantu rencana mengeluarkan Amaterasu dari guanya.
claims.quote: He was one of the principle gods involved in the plan to lure Amaterasu from the cave that she hid herself in.

claims.statement: He is worshipped at Tamanooya Shrine in Yamaguchi.
claims.statement_id: Ia dipuja di Kuil Tamanooya di Yamaguchi.
claims.quote: Tama-no-iwaya is believed to be the grave for the kami, and he is venerated at Tamanooya-jinja in Yamaguchi but is not venerated at any kampeisha.

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki calls him Ninigi’s son.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Shoki menyebutnya putra Ninigi.
claims.quote: The Nihon Shoki states that he was the son of Ninigi, while the Shinsen Shōjiroku says he was the grandson of Takamimusubi.

claims.statement: The Shinsen Shōjiroku instead calls him Takamimusubi’s grandson.
claims.statement_id: Shinsen Shōjiroku justru menyebutnya cucu Takamimusubi.
claims.quote: The Nihon Shoki states that he was the son of Ninigi, while the Shinsen Shōjiroku says he was the grandson of Takamimusubi.

claims.statement: According to the Kokugakuin University Kojiki database synopsis, when Amaterasu shut herself in the rock cave and calamity arose, the eight million deities gathered and planned to coax her out; Tamanooya was responsible for making the string of five hundred jewels of the eight-shaku magatama as one of the ritual implements.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ringkasan basis data Kojiki Universitas Kokugakuin, ketika Amaterasu mengurung diri di gua dan bencana terjadi, delapan juta dewa berkumpul merencanakan membujuknya keluar; Tamanooya bertugas membuat untaian lima ratus permata magatama berukuran delapan shaku sebagai salah satu perlengkapan ritual.
claims.quote: 天照大御神が石屋に籠り、災いが起こった時に、八百万神が天安河原に集まり、石屋から招き出す計画をした。その際、玉祖命は、祭具の一つ、八尺の勾璁の五百津の御すまるの珠の製作を担った。

claims.statement: In the descent of the heavenly grandchild he followed Ninigi down as one of the five itomo-no-o with Ame no Koyane, Futodama, Ame no Uzume and Ishikoridome; he is ancestor of the Tamanooya no Muraji.
claims.statement_id: Dalam bagian turunnya cucu langit, ia mengikuti turunnya Ninigi sebagai salah satu dari lima itomo-no-o bersama Ame no Koyane, Futodama, Ame no Uzume, dan Ishikoridome; ia leluhur Tamanooya no Muraji.
claims.quote: 天孫降臨の段では、五伴緒（天児屋命・布刀玉命・天宇受売命・伊斯許理度売命・玉祖命）の一柱として邇々芸命の降臨に従った。玉祖連らの祖。

claims.statement: The Tamanooya no Muraji, who take him as ancestral deity, are thought to be a clan that headed the jewel-making groups and served the court, and the deity's name is understood as ancestor of a jewel-making tribe.
claims.statement_id: Tamanooya no Muraji, klan yang memujanya sebagai leluhur, dianggap klan pengawas kelompok pembuat permata yang mengabdi kepada istana, dan nama dewa ini dipahami sebagai leluhur suku pembuat permata.
claims.quote: 玉祖命を祖神とする玉祖連は、玉類の生産を担う玉作部を統括し朝廷に仕えた伴造氏族と考えられ、玉祖命という神名も、玉を作る部族の祖先といった意味に解されている。

claims.statement: The reading "Tamanooya" is rivaled by "Tamanoya", since the Nihon Shoki has "Tamanoya no Mikoto" and Old Japanese commonly contracts vowel sequences.
claims.statement_id: Bacaan "Tamanooya" disaingi bacaan "Tamanoya", karena Nihon Shoki menulis "Tamanoya no Mikoto" dan bahasa kuno lazim meringkas rangkaian vokal.
claims.quote: 「玉祖」の読みは、タマノオヤとする説と、『日本書紀』に「玉屋（たまのや）命」とあることや、上代語では母音の連続を約めるのが一般的であることから（ノオ→ノ）、タマノヤとする説とがある。

claims.statement: The Engishiki lists two shrines enshrining Tamanooya; one is the Tamanooya Shrine in Suō Province (Hōfu, Yamaguchi) in Tamanooya-gō, thought to be the shrine of the Tamanooya clan.
claims.statement_id: Engishiki mencatat dua kuil pemuja Tamanooya; salah satunya Tamanooya Jinja di Provinsi Suō (Hōfu, Yamaguchi) di Tamanooya-gō, kuil yang dipercaya dipuja klan Tamanooya.
claims.quote: 『延喜式』神名帳には、玉祖命を祭る神社が二社見える。周防国佐波郡「玉祖神社」二座（山口県防府市）は、玉祖郷に鎮座し、玉祖氏が祭った神社とされる。

claims.statement: According to the shrine's tradition, after following the descent of the heavenly grandchild he developed that land, and after his death his descendants worshipped him, which was the shrine's beginning.
claims.statement_id: Menurut tradisi kuil, setelah mengikuti turunnya cucu langit ia membangun daerah itu, dan setelah ia wafat keturunannya memujanya, itulah awal kuil tersebut.
claims.quote: 社伝では、玉祖命が天孫降臨に従った後、この地を経営し、亡くなった後にその子孫が祭ったのが神社の始まりであるという。

claims.statement: Ubagabi is a ghost light in Kawachi and Tanba legends.
claims.statement_id: Ubagabi adalah cahaya gaib dalam legenda Kawachi dan Tanba.
claims.quote: The ubagabi (姥ヶ火 or 姥火, "old woman's fire") is an atmospheric ghost light in legends of Kawachi Province (now Osaka Prefecture) and Tanba Province (now northern Kyoto Prefecture).

claims.statement: One account describes a ball of fire on rainy nights at Hiraoka.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menggambarkan bola api pada malam hujan di Hiraoka.
claims.quote: According to the Shokoku Rijin Dan, on a rainy night, in Hiraoka, Kawachi (now Higashiōsaka, Osaka Prefecture), it would appear as a ball of fire with a length of one shaku (about 30 centimeters).

claims.statement: An origin tale links it to an old woman who steals shrine oil.
claims.statement_id: Cerita asal menghubungkannya dengan perempuan tua yang mencuri minyak kuil.
claims.quote: It is said that in the past, an old woman stole oil from Hiraoka Shrine and became a mysterious fire from a resulting curse.

claims.statement: A traveler’s account gives it a bird-like appearance.
claims.statement_id: Kisah pelancong memberinya penampilan seperti burung.
claims.quote: Once, when someone was walking along the road at night in Kawachi, the ubagabi suddenly appeared from nowhere and hit this person's face, and when this person looked closely, it took on the form of a chicken-like bird.

claims.statement: It returns to a fireball form when flying away.
claims.statement_id: Ia kembali ke wujud bola api ketika terbang pergi.
claims.quote: It is said that when the ubagabi eventually flew away, it turned back into its original appearance as a ball of fire.

claims.statement: Mizuki Shigeru proposed that it might be a bird.
claims.statement_id: Mizuki Shigeru mengusulkan bahwa ia mungkin burung.
claims.quote: From this, the yōkai manga artist Mizuki Shigeru suggested the possibility that the ubagabi was actually a bird.

claims.statement: Yokai.com writes the name as 姥ヶ火, translates it "old hag fire", and gives the habitat as riverbanks.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menulis namanya 姥ヶ火, menerjemahkannya "api nenek tua", dan menyebut habitatnya tepi sungai.
claims.quote: Ubagabi 姥ヶ火 うばがび Translation: old hag fire Habitat: riverbanks

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the ubagabi is a fireball (hi-no-tama) yokai that appears on rainy nights near riverbanks as a ball of flame about 1 foot across with an old woman's face in it; it can also appear as a chicken but does not remain so for long.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ubagabi adalah yōkai bola api (hi-no-tama) yang muncul pada malam hujan di dekat tepi sungai, berupa bola api berdiameter sekitar 1 kaki dengan wajah nenek di dalamnya; ia juga dapat tampil sebagai ayam tetapi tidak lama.
claims.quote: Ubagabi is a kind of hi-no-tama, or fireball yokai. It appears on rainy nights near riverbanks, and takes the form of a 1 foot diameter ball of flame with the face of an old woman in it. It can also appear as a chicken, but does not remain in this form for long.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, ubagabi are created out of the ghosts of old women who were caught stealing oil and died of shame.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ubagabi tercipta dari hantu nenek-nenek yang tertangkap mencuri minyak dan mati karena malu.
claims.quote: They are created out of the ghosts of old women who were caught stealing oil and died of shame.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, ubagabi can fly long distances, up to 4 kilometers, in the blink of an eye; they sometimes graze a person's shoulder, and that person invariably dies within three years.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ubagabi dapat terbang jauh, hingga 4 kilometer, dalam sekejap; kadang menyerempet bahu seseorang, dan orang itu pasti mati dalam waktu tiga tahun.
claims.quote: Ubagabi have the uncanny ability to fly long distances — up to 4 kilometers — in the blink of an eye. Occasionally they graze a person’s shoulder and then continue off into the darkness. The unfortunate people whom they bounce off of invariably end up dying somehow within three years.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, if one is quick enough to shout "Abura-sashi!" (oil thief) as an ubagabi comes flying, the yokai will vanish.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, bila orang cukup cepat berseru "Abura-sashi!" (pencuri minyak) saat ubagabi melayang ke arahnya, yōkai itu lenyap.
claims.quote: However, if one is quick enough and shouts, “Abura-sashi!” (oil thief) just as an ubagabi comes flying towards him or her, the yokai will vanish.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, the pond behind Hiraoka shrine is known by locals as "Ubagabi-ike" (the pond of the ubagabi).
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, kolam di belakang Kuil Hiraoka oleh penduduk setempat disebut "Ubagabi-ike" (kolam ubagabi).
claims.quote: To this day, the pond behind Hiraoka shrine is known by locals as “Ubagabi-ike” (the pond of the ubagabi)

claims.statement: In one tale the old woman experienced a flood and drowned, after which a mysterious flame is said to have appeared near the Hozu River and people called it the ubagabi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam salah satu kisah, nenek tua itu mengalami banjir dan tenggelam, lalu dikatakan api misterius muncul di dekat Sungai Hozu dan orang menyebutnya ubagabi.
claims.quote: Eventually, perhaps as divine punishment, the old woman experienced a flood and drowned. After that, it is said that a mysterious flame would appear near Hozu River, and people called this the ubagabi.

claims.statement: In the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō it is depicted with an old woman's face within the flames, and the statement "it's said to be in Kawachi Province" makes it a depiction of a Kawachi legend.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Gazu Hyakki Yagyō ia digambarkan dengan wajah nenek di dalam api, dan keterangan "dikatakan di Provinsi Kawachi" menjadikannya gambaran legenda Kawachi.
claims.quote: It is also titled "Ubagabi" (here written as 姥が火) in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō, and it is depicted with an old woman's face within the mysterious flames, but since there is the statement "it's said to be in Kawachi Province" within accompanying description, this makes it a depiction of a Kawachi Province legend.

claims.statement: Umi zatō is a yōkai in Sekien’s collection and illustrated scrolls.
claims.statement_id: Umi zatō adalah yōkai dalam kumpulan Sekien dan gulungan bergambar.
claims.quote: Umi zatō (海座頭 ) is a Japanese yōkai, or supernatural being, in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō by Toriyama Sekien and in various emakimono such as the Matsui Library's Hyakki Yagyō Emaki.

claims.statement: Its image resembles a giant musician standing on the sea.
claims.statement_id: Gambarnya menyerupai pemusik raksasa yang berdiri di laut.
claims.quote: In yōkai depictions, they are depicted looking like a giant biwa hōshi standing above the sea holding a rod in the right hand and carrying a pipa on their back.

claims.statement: The figure carries a rod and an instrument on its back.
claims.statement_id: Sosok itu membawa tongkat dan alat musik di punggung.
claims.quote: In yōkai depictions, they are depicted looking like a giant biwa hōshi standing above the sea holding a rod in the right hand and carrying a pipa on their back.

claims.statement: The early pictures lack explanatory text.
claims.statement_id: Gambar awal tidak memiliki keterangan.
claims.quote: There is no accompanying explanatory text in the Gazu Hyakki Yagyō or Hyakki Yagyō Emaki , so it is unknown what kind of yōkai this was intended to be.

claims.statement: A researcher interprets it as a figure confined to paintings.
claims.statement_id: Seorang peneliti menafsirkannya sebagai sosok yang hanya terdapat dalam lukisan.
claims.quote: considers it a yōkai that has existed only in these paintings.

claims.statement: Postwar interpretations associate it with umibōzu.
claims.statement_id: Tafsir pascaperang menghubungkannya dengan umibōzu.
claims.quote: In books published in the postwar era, there has been the interpretation that this is a kind of umibōzu, which frequently appear off the coast of Sanriku, Rikuchū Province (now Iwate prefecture).

claims.statement: Yokai.com translates the name "blind man of the sea", gives the habitat as the waters surrounding Japan, and its diet as ships and sailors.
claims.statement_id: Yokai.com menerjemahkan nama itu "orang buta dari laut", menyebut habitatnya perairan di sekitar Jepang, dan "makanannya" kapal serta pelaut.
claims.quote: Umi zatō 海座頭 うみざとう Translation: blind man of the sea Habitat: the waters surrounding Japan Diet: ships and sailors

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, umi zatō are mysterious gigantic yokai that look like blind zatō, wandering the seas at night tapping the waves with long canes.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, umi zatō adalah yōkai raksasa misterius yang tampak seperti zatō buta, mengembara di laut pada malam hari dan mengetuk ombak dengan tongkat panjang.
claims.quote: Umi zatō are mysterious, gigantic yokai which look like blind guilds-men, or zatō, who wander the seas at night, tapping the waves with their long canes.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, very little is known about it and it is usually considered harmless and leaves people alone.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, sedikit yang diketahui tentangnya dan ia biasanya dianggap tidak berbahaya dan membiarkan orang.
claims.quote: Very little is known about the mysterious umi zatō. They are usually considered to be harmless and leave people alone.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, it is said to beckon ships near and then flip them over and capsize them, and occasionally swallows entire boats whole.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ia dikatakan memanggil kapal mendekat lalu membalikkannya hingga tenggelam, dan kadang menelan seluruh perahu.
claims.quote: They are said to beckon ships towards them, and when the ships draw close, they flip them over and capsize them. They also occasionally swallow entire boats whole.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, if the people on a ship reply to an umi zatō politely and docilely, it will vanish and leave them alone.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, bila orang di kapal menjawab umi zatō dengan sopan dan patuh, ia lenyap dan membiarkan mereka.
claims.quote: They do have a congenial side, however. If the people on a ship reply to an umi zatō in a polite and docile manner, the umi zatō will vanish and leave them alone.

claims.statement: According to Yokai.com, it is sometimes considered a cousin of the similar-looking umi-bōzu, but is very likely a yokai invented by Edo-period artists solely to decorate old picture scrolls.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Yokai.com, ia kadang dianggap sepupu umi-bōzu yang mirip, tetapi sangat mungkin yōkai rekaan seniman zaman Edo hanya untuk menghias gulungan lukisan.
claims.quote: They are sometimes considered to be cousins of the similar-looking umi-bōzu, but it is very likely that umi zatō is an invented yokai thought up by Edo-period artists solely for decorating old picture scrolls.

claims.statement: According to the Digital Daijisen Plus, the umi zatō is a Japanese yōkai depicted standing on the sea as a monk-like figure with a staff and a biwa on its back, and is described in a Hyakki Yagyō scroll and in Toriyama Sekien's Gazu Hyakki Yagyō.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Digital Daijisen Plus, umi zatō adalah yōkai Jepang yang digambarkan berdiri di atas laut berwujud biksu dengan tongkat dan biwa di punggung, dan tercatat dalam gulungan Hyakki Yagyō dan Gazu Hyakki Yagyō karya Toriyama Sekien.
claims.quote: 海座頭(うみざとう) 日本の妖怪。海上に立つ、杖を持ち琵琶を背負った坊主姿で描かれる。江戸時代の妖怪絵巻「百鬼夜行絵巻」、鳥山石燕(せきえん)の画集「画図百鬼夜行」に記述がある。

claims.statement: Although counted among the umibōzu, their times of appearance differ: they appear when umibōzu no longer do, often at the end of the month.
claims.statement_id: Meski dihitung sebagai umibōzu, waktu kemunculannya berbeda: ia muncul ketika umibōzu tidak muncul lagi, sering pada akhir bulan.
claims.quote: Although they are counted among the umibōzu , their times of appearance are different, appearing at the times when umibōzu no longer appear, often at the end of the month.

claims.statement: They walk around on top of the water, threaten fishermen, beckon ships to make them capsize, and sometimes swallow ships whole.
claims.statement_id: Mereka berjalan di atas air, mengancam nelayan, memanggil kapal agar terbalik, dan kadang menelan kapal bulat-bulat.
claims.quote: They walk around on top of the water, threaten fishermen and beckon ships to make them capsize, and sometimes even swallow ships whole.

claims.statement: It is said that if the umi zatō's words are answered properly, it will go away.
claims.statement_id: Dikatakan bila kata-kata umi zatō dijawab dengan benar, ia akan pergi.
claims.quote: However, it is said that if the umi zatō 's words are answered properly, then it will go away.

claims.statement: Wakahirume is a Japanese goddess associated with the rising sun.
claims.statement_id: Wakahirume adalah dewi Jepang yang dikaitkan dengan matahari terbit.
claims.quote: Wakahirume is a goddess of the rising sun in Japanese mythology in Shinto mythology.

claims.statement: Accounts call her Amaterasu’s daughter or younger sister.
claims.statement_id: Kisah-kisah menyebutnya putri atau adik perempuan Amaterasu.
claims.quote: She is the daughter or younger sister of the sun goddess Amaterasu.

claims.statement: One interpretation sees her as the morning sun personified.
claims.statement_id: Satu tafsir melihatnya sebagai personifikasi matahari pagi.
claims.quote: Some interpretations view her as the personification of the morning sun.

claims.statement: She makes garments for the kami.
claims.statement_id: Ia membuat pakaian bagi para kami.
claims.quote: She was involved in making garments for the kami.

claims.statement: A Nihongi account has her killed by Susanoo’s attack in the weaving hall.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Nihongi menyebutnya terbunuh akibat serangan Susanoo di balai tenun.
claims.quote: In some versions Wakahirume was killed when Susanoo threw a flayed pony at her while she was in Amaterasu's weaving hall as written in the Nihongi.

claims.statement: Another tradition has her request residence in Ikuta Nagao.
claims.statement_id: Tradisi lain menyebutnya meminta tinggal di Ikuta Nagao.
claims.quote: Wakahirume no mikoto appeared and there was a divine message, 'I would like to stay in Ikuta Nagao no kuni'.

claims.statement: According to Nipponica, in one variant of Susanoo's misconduct in the Nihon Shoki, Wakahirume is the deity who is wounded by a shuttle when Susanoo throws a backward-flayed horse into the weaving hall, and departs.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nipponica, dalam satu riwayat kelakuan Susanoo di Nihon Shoki, Wakahirume adalah dewi yang terluka oleh teropong tenun karena Susanoo melempar kuda yang dikuliti terbalik ke balai tenun, lalu pergi.
claims.quote: 書紀神話の素戔嗚尊(すさのおのみこと)乱行の一伝で、尊(みこと)が逆剥(さかは)ぎの馬を織機殿(はたどの)に投げ入れたために梭(ひ)で傷ついて去る神。

claims.statement: Because in the main text of the Nihon Shoki the story concerns Amaterasu, also called Ōhirume, Wakahirume is considered an offshoot (bunshin) of Amaterasu.
claims.statement_id: Karena dalam teks utama Nihon Shoki kisah itu menyangkut Amaterasu yang juga disebut Ōhirume, Wakahirume dianggap sebagai bagian-diri (bunshin) Amaterasu.
claims.quote: 紀本文では、大日孁(おおひるめ)ともよばれる天照大神(あまてらすおおみかみ)の話となっているため、ここの稚日女尊はその分身と考えられる。

claims.statement: In the Nihon Shoki's opening section on Empress Jingū, she names herself the deity of Awa no kōri in Oda, gives an oracle at Muko together with Amaterasu, Kotoshironushi and the three Sumiyoshi deities, and is enshrined at Ikuta Shrine (Kobe) by Unakami no Isachi.
claims.statement_id: Dalam bagian awal Permaisuri Jingū Nihon Shoki, ia menyebut dirinya dewa di Awa no kōri di Ota, memberi wahyu di Muko bersama Amaterasu, Kotoshironushi, dan tiga dewa Sumiyoshi, lalu dipuja di Kuil Ikuta (Kobe) oleh Unakami no Isachi.
claims.quote: この尊は『神功(じんぐう)摂政前紀』にも「尾田の吾田節(あがたふし)の淡郡(あわのこおり)にある神」と名のり、皇后の半島平定後ふたたび天照大神、事代主神(ことしろぬしのかみ)、住吉(すみよし)三神とともに武庫(むこ)（武器庫）で託宣し、海上五十狭茅(うなかみのいさち)によって生田(いくた)神社（神戸市）に祀(まつ)られる。

claims.statement: According to Heibonsha, Ikuta Shrine enshrines Wakahirume; per the Nihon Shoki, when Empress Jingū's ship would not move at Muko, Wakahirume told that she should be enshrined in the land of Ikuta Nagao, and Unakami no Isachi was ordered to enshrine her.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Heibonsha, Kuil Ikuta memuja Wakahirume; menurut Nihon Shoki, ketika kapal Permaisuri Jingū tidak bergerak di Muko, Wakahirume memerintahkan agar ia dipuja di negeri Ikuta Nagao, dan Unakami no Isachi diperintahkan memujanya.
claims.quote: 稚日女（わかひるめ）尊をまつる。《日本書紀》によると神功皇后が外征より凱旋するとき，武庫の水門で船が進まなくなったので占ったところ稚日女尊の〈吾を活田（いくた）の長峡（ながお）の国に祀れ〉との教えがあり，海上五十狭茅（うなかみのいさち）に命じてまつらせた。

claims.statement: According to Kodansha, while weaving clothing in the sacred hall she was startled by the backward-flayed horse thrown by Susanoo, wounded by the shuttle and died; for that reason Amaterasu hid herself in the Heavenly Rock-cave.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kodansha, saat menenun pakaian di balai suci ia terkejut oleh kuda terbalik yang dilempar Susanoo, terluka teropong, dan mati; karena itu Amaterasu bersembunyi di gua langit.
claims.quote: 斎服殿(いみはたどの)で衣を織っているとき,素戔嗚尊(すさのおのみこと)がなげいれた逆剥(さかは)ぎの馬におどろき,梭(ひ)で傷ついて死んだ。そのため天照大神(あまてらすおおみかみ)は天岩窟(あまのいわや)に身をかくしてしまう。

claims.statement: In Aston's translation of the Nihongi, Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto was in the sacred weaving-hall weaving the garments of the Deities when Sosa no wo no Mikoto flung a piebald colt flayed backward into the hall.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Aston atas Nihongi, Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto sedang menenun pakaian para dewa di balai tenun suci ketika Sosa no wo no Mikoto melemparkan anak kuda belang yang dikuliti terbalik ke dalam balai.
claims.quote: After this Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto was in the sacred weaving-hall, weaving the garments of the Deities. Sosa no wo no Mikoto saw this, and forthwith flaying a piebald colt with a backward flaying, flung it into the interior of the hall.

claims.statement: Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto was startled, fell from the loom, wounded herself with the shuttle in her hand, and "divinely departed".
claims.statement_id: Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto terkejut, jatuh dari alat tenun, melukai dirinya dengan teropong di tangannya, dan "pergi secara ilahi" (wafat).
claims.quote: Then Waka-hiru-me no Mikoto was startled, and fell down from the loom, wounding herself with the shuttle which she held in her hand, and divinely departed.

claims.statement: Wani is a sea monster or dragon in Japanese mythology.
claims.statement_id: Wani adalah monster laut atau naga dalam mitologi Jepang.
claims.quote: Wani (鰐) was a dragon or sea monster in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: Translations variously use crocodile or shark.
claims.statement_id: Terjemahan memakai buaya atau hiu.
claims.quote: Since it is written using the kanji 鰐 (from Chinese e 鰐 or 鱷 "crocodile; alligator") wani is translated as "crocodile", or sometimes "shark" (from wanizame 鰐鮫 "shark").

claims.statement: Classical texts write its name in phonetic characters and a crocodile character.
claims.statement_id: Teks klasik menulis namanya dengan aksara fonetik dan aksara buaya.
claims.quote: They write wani with the Man'yōgana phonetic transcription 和邇 and the kanji 鰐.

claims.statement: The Kojiki uses wani both as a proper name and a sea monster.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki memakai wani sebagai nama diri maupun monster laut.
claims.quote: The Kojiki uses wani 和邇 several times as a proper name (e.g., the Confucianist scholar Wani) and as a sea-monster in two contexts.

claims.statement: Wani is a fundamental theme in the myth of the demigod brothers Hoori and Hoderi: the sea god Watatsumi or Ryūjin summons all the wani and chooses one to escort his pregnant daughter Toyotama-hime and her husband Hoori from the palace back to land.
claims.statement_id: Wani adalah tema pokok dalam mitos saudara-saudara setengah dewa Hoori dan Hoderi: dewa laut Watatsumi atau Ryūjin mengumpulkan semua wani, lalu memilih satu untuk mengantar putrinya Toyotama-hime yang sedang hamil dan suaminya Hoori dari istana kembali ke daratan.
claims.quote: Second, wani is a fundamental theme in the myth of the demigod brothers Hoori and Hoderi. The sea god Watatsumi or Ryūjin "summoned together all the crocodiles" and chose one to escort his pregnant daughter Toyotama-hime and her husband Hoori from the Ryūgū-jō palace back to land.

claims.statement: The sea god's daughter makes a request concerning her shapeshifting into a wani, and at the moment of delivery she turns into a "crocodile" eight fathoms long that crawls and writhes about.
claims.statement_id: Putri dewa laut meminta agar ia dapat berubah menjadi wani, dan pada saat melahirkan ia berubah menjadi "buaya" sepanjang delapan depa yang merayap dan menggeliat.
claims.quote: the beautiful Toyatama-hime made a bizarre request concerning her shapeshifting into a wani ... when she turned into a crocodile eight fathoms [long], and crawled and writhed about

claims.statement: In the tale of the White Hare of Inaba, told by the hare, the wani are tricked into lying in a row; the hare treads on them while counting, and the wani lying last seizes it and strips off all its "clothing".
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Kelinci Putih dari Inaba yang dituturkan sang kelinci, wani ditipu sehingga berbaris di laut; kelinci itu menginjak mereka sambil menghitung, dan wani yang berbaring paling akhir menyambar serta melucuti "pakaian" kelinci itu.
claims.quote: they were deceived and lay down in a row, and I trod on them and counted them as I came across, and was just about to get on land, when I said: 'You have been deceived by me.' As soon as I had finished speaking, the crocodile who lay the last of all seized me and stripped off all my clothing. ... This was the White Hare of Inaba.

claims.statement: The Nihongi uses the word kuma-wani ("bear-wani", i.e. giant or strong) and describes the sea god Kotoshiro-nushi as a ya-hiro no kuma-wani, an "8-fathom bear-wani".
claims.statement_id: Nihongi memakai kata kuma-wani ("wani beruang", yaitu raksasa atau kuat) dan menyebut dewa laut Kotoshironushi sebagai ya-hiro no kuma-wani, "wani beruang sepanjang delapan depa".
claims.quote: The Nihongi likewise uses wani several times as a proper name ... and twice in the word kuma-wani 熊鰐 "bear (i.e., giant or strong) shark/crocodile". First, the mythical sea god Kotoshiro-nushi-no-kami (see Ebisu) is described as a ya-hiro no kuma-wani 八尋熊鰐 "8-fathom bear-wani"

claims.statement: Aston wrote that there can be little doubt that the wani is really the Chinese dragon, which is frequently so represented in Japanese pictures.
claims.statement_id: Aston menulis bahwa hampir pasti wani sebenarnya adalah naga Tiongkok, yang sering digambarkan demikian dalam gambar Jepang.
claims.quote: Aston later wrote that. There can be little doubt that the wani is really the Chinese dragon. It is frequently so represented in Japanese pictures.

claims.statement: De Visser discussed the wani in detail and gave his opinion that the wani is an old Japanese dragon- or serpent-shaped sea-god.
claims.statement_id: De Visser membahas wani secara rinci dan berpendapat bahwa wani adalah dewa laut Jepang kuno berwujud naga atau ular.
claims.quote: Marinus Willem de Visser discussed the wani in detail. ... In my opinion the wani is an old Japanese dragon- or serpent-shaped sea-god

claims.statement: Chamberlain justified translating wani as "crocodile" in a footnote, judging that the accounts point to an amphibious creature somewhat similar to the serpent rather than to a fish.
claims.statement_id: Chamberlain membenarkan terjemahan "buaya" dalam catatan kaki dan menilai bahwa keterangan lama menunjuk pada makhluk amfibi yang agak mirip ular, bukan ikan.
claims.quote: Chamberlain justified translating "crocodile" in a footnote. ... the accounts point rather to an amphibious creature, conceived of as being somewhat similar to the serpent, than to a fish

claims.statement: Aston, who argued against translating wani as "crocodile", held that the wani inhabits the sea and not rivers and is plainly a mythical creature.
claims.statement_id: Aston berpendapat bahwa wani tinggal di laut dan bukan di sungai, dan jelas merupakan makhluk mitos; karena itu ia tidak menerjemahkannya sebagai "buaya".
claims.quote: William George Aston justified not translating wani as "crocodile". ... The wani, too, inhabits the sea and not rivers, and is plainly a mythical creature.

claims.statement: According to the Heibonsha encyclopedia entry, applying the Japanese word wani to the crocodile was an error of ancient central literati; wani is a San'in-region dialect word for the large shark (fuka), and there is a longline fishery for wani.
claims.statement_id: Menurut entri ensiklopedia Heibonsha, penerapan kata Jepang wani pada buaya adalah kekeliruan para sastrawan pusat Jepang kuno; wani adalah dialek wilayah San'in untuk hiu besar (fuka), dan di sana ada penangkapan wani dengan tali pancing panjang.
claims.quote: 日本語のワニをこれに当てたのは古代日本の中央文人の誤りで，山陰地方における鱶（ふか）の方言であり，ワニのはえなわ漁がある。

claims.statement: The same entry says the Izumo no Kuni Fudoki also has a legend of a wani that, in love with the deity of a mountain village in Nita District, tried to swim up the river.
claims.statement_id: Menurut entri yang sama, Izumo no Kuni Fudoki memuat legenda wani yang mencintai dewa sebuah desa di pegunungan Distrik Nita dan mencoba menyusuri sungai ke hulu.
claims.quote: 神聖な魚とみられたのであろう。《出雲国風土記》にも仁多郡の山間の阿伊村の神を恋うワニが川をさかのぼろうとしたという伝説がある。

claims.statement: The Hizen no Kuni Fudoki records a tradition that a wani went up a river to the place where a deity was, with many sea fish following it.
claims.statement_id: Hizen no Kuni Fudoki mencatat tradisi bahwa wani menyusuri sungai ke tempat dewa berada, dan banyak ikan laut mengikutinya.
claims.quote: 《肥前国風土記》でもワニが川をさかのぼって神のいる場所にいき，海魚が多くこれに従うという伝承を記している。

claims.statement: In Izumo City, when a wani (shark) was caught, the pectoral fin and cheek meat of one fish were customarily taken to the Ono family at Hinomisaki; the author surmises it was regarded as a sacred fish.
claims.statement_id: Di Kota Izumo, ketika wani (hiu) ditangkap, sirip dada dan daging pipi seekor ikan dahulu dibawa ke keluarga Ono di Hinomisaki; penulis menduga ikan itu dipandang sebagai ikan suci.
claims.quote: 出雲市ではかまぼこの材料はモバワニの肉がよいといい，これを捕獲するとその1尾のワイワビ（脇鰭）と頰肉とを切り取って日御碕（ひのみさき）の小野家に持参する習わしがあった。神聖な魚とみられたのであろう。

claims.statement: In this Nihongi translation, Toyo-tama-hime changes into an enormous "sea-monster" of eight fathoms that wriggles about on her belly.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Nihongi ini, Toyo-tama-hime berubah menjadi "monster laut" raksasa sepanjang delapan depa yang menggeliat di atas perutnya.
claims.quote: At this time Toyo-tama-hime had become changed into an enormous sea-monster of eight fathoms, and was wriggling about on her belly.

claims.statement: In this Nihongi translation, the courser on which the Sea-God rides is a sea-monster eight fathoms in length who stays with fins erect in the small orange-tree house.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Nihongi ini, tunggangan Dewa Laut disebut monster laut sepanjang delapan depa yang berdiri dengan sirip tegak di rumah jeruk kecil.
claims.quote: The courser on which the Sea-God rides is a sea-monster eight fathoms in length, who with fins erect stays in the small orange-tree house.

claims.statement: In this Nihongi translation, the sea-monsters are summoned together, and the one-fathom sea-monsters are sent as his escort.
claims.statement_id: Dalam terjemahan Nihongi ini, para monster laut dikumpulkan, dan monster laut sepanjang satu depa dikirim sebagai pengawal.
claims.quote: Then he summoned together the sea-monsters ... The one-fathom sea-monsters were accordingly sent with him as his escort.

claims.statement: Jing is a category of supernatural spirit in Chinese tradition.
claims.statement_id: Jing adalah kategori roh gaib dalam tradisi Tiongkok.
claims.quote: 精，是一種超自然生命體，在世界各国皆有传说，天地万物皆可能寄宿精。有生物或非生物日积月累变成妖怪的成精，也有本来活在自然环境的自然精灵，有些能幻化成不同形态。

claims.statement: Living beings and objects may develop such spirits over time.
claims.statement_id: Makhluk hidup dan benda dapat mengembangkan roh semacam itu seiring waktu.
claims.quote: 精，是一種超自然生命體，在世界各国皆有传说，天地万物皆可能寄宿精。有生物或非生物日积月累变成妖怪的成精，也有本来活在自然环境的自然精灵，有些能幻化成不同形态。

claims.statement: Some are described as changing into different forms.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian digambarkan dapat berubah menjadi berbagai wujud.
claims.quote: 精，是一種超自然生命體，在世界各国皆有传说，天地万物皆可能寄宿精。有生物或非生物日积月累变成妖怪的成精，也有本来活在自然环境的自然精灵，有些能幻化成不同形态。

claims.statement: Examples include fox, snake, tree and flower spirits.
claims.statement_id: Contohnya meliputi roh rubah, ular, pohon, dan bunga.
claims.quote: 精怪的代表可算狐狸精，其次還有蛇精、樹精和花精等等。稱呼時大多稱為「〔原形名〕+精」。

claims.statement: According to this Chinese Wikipedia article, the Soushenji holds that all things have spirits which over time turn into monsters; Chinese jing have a complete genealogy according to works such as the Baize Jingguai Tu, and include non-living things such as utensils besides animals and plants.
claims.statement_id: Menurut artikel Wikipedia berbahasa Mandarin ini, Soushenji menganggap segala sesuatu memiliki roh yang lama-kelamaan menjadi siluman; jing dalam Tiongkok memiliki silsilah lengkap menurut Baize Jingguai Tu dan sejenisnya, dan selain hewan serta tumbuhan juga mencakup benda mati seperti perkakas.
claims.quote: 东晋干宝搜神记认为万物有灵，久了就会化作妖怪。中国的精，依《白泽精怪图》等书的记载有一个完整的谱系，其中印度的传入也汇进这个谱系。同时，中国的精除动植物之外，也有非生物包括器具，日本的精有较多受中国影响。

claims.statement: It is widely believed that all things, living or not, that live or are kept for a hundred or a thousand years or more absorb the essence of nature and become jing, also called jingguai.
claims.statement_id: Secara umum dipercaya bahwa segala hal, hidup maupun tidak, yang hidup atau tersimpan seratus atau seribu tahun lebih akan menyerap sari alam dan menjadi jing, yang juga disebut jingguai.
claims.quote: 普遍认为各种事物包括生物和非生物，只要活或保存百年、千年以上时间就会吸收自然界的精华成精，亦稱為精怪。

claims.statement: According to Chinese legend, some strange phenomena involving people may be influenced by jingguai; the legends say they have abilities such as transformation and illusion arts and may lodge in certain objects.
claims.statement_id: Menurut legenda Tiongkok, sebagian kejadian ganjil yang berkaitan dengan manusia mungkin dipengaruhi jingguai; legenda menyebut jingguai memiliki kemampuan seperti berubah wujud dan ilmu ilusi, serta dapat bersemayam pada benda-benda tertentu.
claims.quote: 中国传说认为包括与人有关的怪异现象可能有些是精怪影响的，传说精怪会包括变身、幻术等不同能力，还会寄宿在一些物体上。

claims.statement: Besides China, regions such as Japan have a similar concept, for example the legend of old utensils becoming tsukumogami.
claims.statement_id: Selain Tiongkok, Jepang juga memiliki konsep serupa, misalnya legenda perkakas tua yang menjadi tsukumogami.
claims.quote: 除了中国，其他一些地区如日本亦有类似成精的概念，如陈旧器具变「付喪神」的传说。

claims.statement: In Eastern cultures a yaoguai is sometimes called a yaojing, and in speech the characters yao, jing and guai are often used together and sometimes interchangeably.
claims.statement_id: Dalam budaya Timur, yaoguai kadang disebut yaojing, dan dalam percakapan huruf yao, jing, dan guai sering dipakai bersama atau saling menggantikan.
claims.quote: 在东方文化妖怪有时也叫妖精，在口語中，「妖」、「精」、「怪」幾個字經常連用，有時候還能相互替換。

claims.statement: The example given is Sun Wukong in the Xiyouji, a stone that became a jing and turned into a monkey.
claims.statement_id: Contoh yang disebut: Sun Wukong dalam Xiyouji adalah batu yang menjadi jing lalu berubah menjadi monyet.
claims.quote: 然后变成其他生物、非生物或人形态。（如西游记孙悟空就石头成精变猴子）

claims.statement: According to the Baopuzi, the jing of all aged things can all assume human form to dazzle people's eyes and constantly test them, but cannot change their true form in a mirror.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Baopuzi, jing semua benda yang sudah tua dapat menyamar sebagai manusia untuk menyilaukan mata dan terus menguji orang, tetapi tidak dapat mengubah wujud aslinya di dalam cermin.
claims.quote: 又萬物之老者，其精悉能假讬人形，以眩惑人目而常試人，唯不能於鏡中易其真形耳。

claims.statement: According to the Baopuzi, ancient Daoists entering the mountains hung a bright mirror nine cun or more in diameter behind their backs, so that the old spirits (laomei) dared not come near people.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Baopuzi, para daoshi zaman dahulu yang masuk gunung menggantungkan cermin terang berdiameter sembilan cun atau lebih di punggung mereka, sehingga laomei (siluman tua) tidak berani mendekat.
claims.quote: 是以古之入山道士，皆以明鏡徑九寸已上，懸於背後，則老魅不敢近人。

claims.statement: According to the Baopuzi, if the visitor is a bird- or beast-spirit its form shows in the mirror; an old spirit that comes also leaves walking backwards and has no heels.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Baopuzi, jika yang datang adalah siluman burung atau hewan, wujudnya tampak di cermin; siluman tua yang datang juga pergi dengan berjalan mundur dan tidak punya tumit.
claims.quote: 若是鳥獸邪魅，則其形貌皆見鏡中矣。又老魅若來，其去必卻行，行可轉鏡對之，其後而視之，若是老魅者，必無踵也

claims.statement: In a Baopuzi tale of two men in a stone chamber, a visitor dressed as a person appears as a deer in the mirror; when addressed as an old deer he turns into a deer and runs off.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Baopuzi tentang dua orang di sebuah gua batu, seorang pengunjung berpakaian seperti manusia tampak sebagai rusa di cermin; ketika ditegur sebagai rusa tua, ia berubah menjadi rusa dan lari.
claims.quote: 於是二人顧視鏡中，乃是鹿也。因問之曰：汝是山中老鹿，何敢詐為人形。言未絕，而來人即成鹿而走去。

claims.statement: According to a saying quoted in the Soushenji from the Baize Tu, between two mountains there is a jing like a small child named Xinang that stretches out a hand to pull people, and it dies if drawn away from its old place.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ucapan yang dikutip dalam Soushenji dari Baize Tu, di antara dua gunung ada jing berupa anak kecil bernama Xinang yang mengulurkan tangan untuk menarik orang, dan ia mati bila ditarik dari tempat asalnya.
claims.quote: 此事在白澤圖內；曰：『兩山之間，其精如小兒，見人，則伸手欲引人，名曰「傒囊」，引去故地，則死。

claims.statement: The Soushenji quotes a saying that the jing of wood is "Youguang" and the jing of metal is "Qingming".
claims.statement_id: Soushenji mengutip ucapan bahwa jing kayu adalah "Youguang" dan jing logam adalah "Qingming".
claims.quote: 索縛，則可得食。」王子曰：「木精為『游光』，金精為『清明』也。」

claims.statement: Yakusanoikazuchi is the collective name of eight thunder kami.
claims.statement_id: Yakusanoikazuchi adalah nama kolektif delapan kami petir.
claims.quote: Yakusanoikazuchi or ikazuchi is a collective name for the eight kami of thunder in Japanese mythology.

claims.statement: The deities represent different forms of storm.
claims.statement_id: Para dewa itu mewakili berbagai bentuk badai.
claims.quote: Each one represents a different type of storm.

claims.statement: The element ikazuchi means thunder.
claims.statement_id: Unsur ikazuchi berarti petir.
claims.quote: Ikazuchi (雷) literally means thunder in Japanese.

claims.statement: Some tellings say the eight deities came from the maggots of Izanami's rotting corpse.
claims.statement_id: Beberapa penuturan menyebut kedelapan dewa itu berasal dari belatung jasad Izanami yang membusuk.
claims.quote: Some tellings say that the eight deities were from the maggots of Izanami's rotting corpse.

claims.statement: They pursue Izanagi when he flees the underworld.
claims.statement_id: Mereka mengejar Izanagi ketika ia melarikan diri dari alam kematian.
claims.quote: Many versions of the Nihon Shoki and the Kojiki state that after Izanagi saw his wife in such a state and fled in terror, Izanami sent the Yomotsu-shikome, 150 warriors, and the eight thunder kami after him.

claims.statement: The Kojiki places Black Thunder in Izanami’s belly.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menempatkan Petir Hitam di perut Izanami.
claims.quote: Kuro-ikazuchi: (Black thunder) The Kojiki says that this deity came from Izanami's belly.

claims.statement: The Nihon Shoki instead places Black Thunder in her rectum.
claims.statement_id: Nihon Shoki justru menempatkan Petir Hitam di duburnya.
claims.quote: However, the Nihon Shoki says that Kuro-ikazuchi was in Izanami's rectum.

claims.statement: According to the Encyclopedia of Shinto, the Yakusa no ikazuchi no kami of the Kojiki are the "eight kinds of thunder kami" that festered inside Izanami's corpse as seen by her consort Izanagi in the underworld of Yomi.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Ensiklopedia Shinto, Yakusa no ikazuchi no kami dalam Kojiki adalah "delapan jenis kami petir" yang membusuk di dalam jasad Izanami, seperti dilihat suaminya Izanagi di dunia bawah Yomi.
claims.quote: [Yakusa no ikazuchi no kami] (Kojiki) The "eight kinds of thunder kami" that festered inside Izanami's corpse as seen by her consort Izanagi in the underworld of Yomi.

claims.statement: According to the Kojiki, the eight thunders were in the corpse's head (great thunder), breast (fire thunder), belly (black thunder), genitals (cleft thunder), left hand (young thunder), right hand (earth thunder), left leg (sounding thunder) and right leg (reposing thunder).
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kojiki, kedelapan petir itu berada di kepala (petir besar), dada (petir api), perut (petir hitam), kemaluan (petir belah), tangan kiri (petir muda), tangan kanan (petir tanah), kaki kiri (petir bergema), dan kaki kanan (petir beristirahat) Izanami.
claims.quote: According to Kojiki, in her head was the "great thunder," in her breast was the "fire thunder," in her belly was the "black thunder," in her genitals was the "cleft thunder," in her left hand was the "young thunder," in the right hand was the "earth thunder," in her left leg was the "sounding thunder," and in her right leg was the "reposing thunder."

claims.statement: An "alternate writing" transmitted by the Nihongi states that great thunder was in her head, fire thunder in her breast, earth thunder in her belly, young thunder in her back, black thunder in her rectum, mountain thunder in her hands, field thunder in her feet and cleft thunder in her genitals.
claims.statement_id: Satu "tulisan alternatif" dalam Nihongi menyebut petir besar di kepala, petir api di dada, petir tanah di perut, petir muda di punggung, petir hitam di dubur, petir gunung di tangan, petir ladang di kaki, dan petir belah di kemaluan.
claims.quote: An "alternate writing" transmitted by Nihongi, however, states that "great thunder" was in her head, "fire thunder" was in her breast, "earth thunder" was in her belly, "young thunder" was in her back, "black thunder" was in her rectum, "mountain thunder" was in her hands, "field thunder" was in her feet, and "cleft thunder" was in her genitals.

claims.statement: Of the eight thunders, three have the same name and place in the two accounts, three agree in name only, and the remaining two are different.
claims.statement_id: Dari delapan petir itu, tiga memiliki nama dan tempat yang sama dalam dua catatan, tiga hanya sama namanya, dan dua sisanya berbeda.
claims.quote: Of the eight thunders, three have the same name and place in the two accounts, three agree in name only, and the remaining two are different.

claims.statement: The eight thunders produced in Izanami's dead body parallel the eight kami produced from the dismembered body of the fire kami Kagutsuchi; eight is considered a sacred number but is here likely used merely to denote "a great many".
claims.statement_id: Lahirnya delapan petir dari jasad Izanami disamakan dengan lahirnya delapan kami dari tubuh Kagutsuchi yang terpotong; delapan dianggap angka suci, tetapi di sini mungkin hanya berarti "sangat banyak".
claims.quote: The fact that eight thunders were produced in Izanami's dead body parallels the fact that eight kami were produced from the dismembered body of the fire kami Kagutsuchi. While eight is considered a sacred number, it is here likely used merely to denote "a great many."

claims.statement: According to the various Kojiki and Nihongi accounts, Izanami ordered the "hags of Yomi" and the eight thunder kami to chase Izanagi; Izanagi threw down magical peaches at Yomotsuhirasaka and thus dispersed his pursuers.
claims.statement_id: Menurut berbagai catatan Kojiki dan Nihongi, Izanami memerintahkan "nenek-nenek Yomi" dan delapan kami petir mengejar Izanagi; Izanagi melempar buah persik gaib di Yomotsuhirasaka dan mengusir para pengejarnya.
claims.quote: According to the various Kojiki and Nihongi accounts mentioned above, Izanami ordered the "hags of Yomi" and the eight thunder kami to chase Izanagi ... Izanagi, however, threw down magical peaches at Yomotsuhirasaka (the "Even Pass of Yomi"), and thus dispersed his pursuers.

claims.statement: The Wikipedia list gives Fusu-ikazuchi (couchant thunder) and Hono-ikazuchi (fire thunder); the Kojiki says Hono-ikazuchi came from Izanami's breasts.
claims.statement_id: Daftar Wikipedia mencantumkan Fusu-ikazuchi (petir berbaring) dan Hono-ikazuchi (petir api); Kojiki menyebut Hono-ikazuchi berasal dari dada Izanami.
claims.quote: Fusu-ikazuchi: (Couchant thunder) Hono-ikazuchi: (Fire thunder) the Kojiki says that this kami came from Izanami's breasts.

claims.statement: Both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki state that Ō-ikazuchi (great thunder) came from Izanami's head.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihon Shoki sama-sama menyebut Ō-ikazuchi (petir besar) berasal dari kepala Izanami.
claims.quote: Ō-ikazuchi: (Great thunder) both the Kojiki and the Nihon Shoki state that Ō-ikazuchi came from Izanami's head.

claims.statement: Yamabito is a mountain-people concept in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Yamabito adalah konsep manusia gunung dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: The term yamabito (山人) or sanjin, as understood in Japanese folklore, has come to be applied to a group, some scholars claim, of ancient, marginalized people, dating back to some unknown date during the Jōmon period of the history of Japan.

claims.statement: The name is translated as mountain people or woodsman.
claims.statement_id: Namanya diterjemahkan sebagai manusia gunung atau penghuni hutan.
claims.quote: The term itself has been translated as "mountain people", or as Dickins interprets the word as "woodsman", but there is more to it than that.

claims.statement: Yanagita interpreted them as descendants of a marginalized ancestral population.
claims.statement_id: Yanagita menafsirkannya sebagai keturunan populasi leluhur yang terpinggirkan.
claims.quote: According to Yanagita, the Yamabito were "descendants of a real, separate aboriginal race of people who were long ago forced into the mountains by the Japanese who then populated the plains" during the Jōmon period.

claims.statement: Yanagita records related folktales in Tono Monogatari.
claims.statement_id: Yanagita mencatat cerita rakyat terkait dalam Tono Monogatari.
claims.quote: Yanagita wrote down these folktales in the book Tono Monogatari

claims.statement: According to Nipponica, residents who once lived in the mountains were called yamabito or yamaotoko by villagers and thought to be descendants of the indigenous people; tales of meeting them were often told in villages until the Meiji era, reflecting farmers' awe of mountain dwellers.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nipponica, penduduk yang dahulu tinggal di pegunungan disebut yamabito atau yamaotoko oleh penduduk desa dan dianggap keturunan penduduk asli; cerita perjumpaan dengan mereka sering dituturkan di desa hingga zaman Meiji, dan mencerminkan rasa takut petani terhadap orang pegunungan.
claims.quote: かつては村人に対して、山中にいた住民を山人または山男とよんで、先住民の子孫と考えられていた。明治時代まで村ではこの人々に出会ったという話がよく伝えられた。町の市(いち)などに現れたとか、山中に大男が寝ていて、脱いだ大きな履き物があったとかいう。農民にとって、山間に住む人への畏怖(いふ)感の反映がみられる。

claims.statement: According to Nipponica, the Tankai (1795) by Tsumura Sōan records that at Hakone in Sagami Province (Kanagawa Prefecture) there was a yamaotoko who was naked, wore leaves and bark, lived deep in the mountains, and made his living catching akahara fish.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Nipponica, Tankai (1795) karya Tsumura Sōan mencatat bahwa di Hakone, Provinsi Sagami (Prefektur Kanagawa), ada seorang yamaotoko yang telanjang, berpakaian daun dan kulit kayu, tinggal di pegunungan dalam, dan mencari ikan akahara.
claims.quote: 江戸時代、津村淙庵(そうあん)の著した『譚海(たんかい)』（1795）に次のような記事がある。 ... 相模(さがみ)国（神奈川県）箱根に山男というものがいた。裸体で木葉樹皮を衣とし深山中に住んで赤腹魚をとるのを業としていた。

claims.statement: In the same account, he knew there was a market, brought the fish to exchange for rice, said little beyond trading, and afterwards returned like a flying bird through places with no road.
claims.statement_id: Menurut kisah yang sama, ia tahu ada pasar, membawa ikan itu untuk ditukar dengan beras, tidak banyak bicara selain berdagang, dan pulang seperti burung terbang lewat tempat tanpa jalan.
claims.quote: 市があるのを知っていてこの魚をもってきて米と交換した。交易のほか多言せず、交易が終わると道のない所を鳥の飛ぶように帰っていった。

claims.statement: According to the Heibonsha World Encyclopedia, traditions about yamabito could be heard in mountain villages across the country, and most are of the yokai kind such as yamaotoko, yamauba, tengu and oni.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Ensiklopedia Dunia Heibonsha, tradisi tentang yamabito bisa didengar di desa pegunungan di seluruh negeri, dan sebagian besar berupa jenis yokai seperti yamaotoko, yamauba, tengu, dan oni.
claims.quote: 山人の伝承は全国の山間の村で聞くことができたが，その多くは山男，山姥（やまうば），天狗，鬼などの妖怪の類である。

claims.statement: According to the same encyclopedia, lowland rice farmers saw the mountains as a foreign space held in awe, which gave rise to many strange occurrences.
claims.statement_id: Menurut ensiklopedia yang sama, penduduk dataran yang bertani padi sawah memandang gunung sebagai ruang asing yang ditakuti, sehingga banyak kejadian ganjil lahir dari sana.
claims.quote: 里に住んで水田稲作農業に従事している人々からは，山は異質の空間であると認識され，畏怖の観念でとらえられていたため，多くの怪異を生み出したのである。

claims.statement: Yanagita assumed that yamabito really existed: indigenous people driven into the mountains by immigrant rice-farming people who worshipped the heavenly kami (amatsukami), non-rice-farmers who worshipped the earthly kami (kunitsukami).
claims.statement_id: Yanagita Kunio berasumsi bahwa yamabito benar-benar ada: penduduk asli yang diusir ke pegunungan oleh bangsa pendatang petani padi pemuja dewa langit (amatsukami), dan mereka adalah orang non-petani padi pemuja dewa bumi (kunitsukami).
claims.quote: 柳田は山人が実在したことを仮定して，天津神（あまつかみ）を奉ずる渡来民族（水田稲作農耕民）によって山に追われた先住民が山人であるとし，山人は国津神（くにつかみ）を奉じた非稲作民であったとしている。

claims.statement: Yanagita named the yamabito's character as honest, scrupulous, brave, stubborn, tenacious, unwilling to lose and vengeful, presenting a rich picture of them.
